title: Estoppel, Equitable
description: Claims for equitable and promissory estoppel differ only in that promissory estoppel applies to the promisor’s representation of future acts and equitable estoppel addresses existing events. See [Crown Life Ins. Co. v. McBride, 517 So. 2d 660, 661-662 (Fla. 1987)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16541373562318926704). A claim for equitable estoppel against the government requires proof of some affirmative misconduct by the government. [Whitaker v. United States, No. 5:18-cv-51-MCR/MJF, 2019 WL 4722465, at *9 (N.D. Fla. August 27, 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1098167881724104410); [Tefel v. Reno, 180 F. 3d 1286, 1303 (11th Cir. 1999)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5504276838858846358).
elements: A representation by defendant (the party estopped), to plaintiff (the party claiming estoppel) as to a material fact;
The representation is contrary to the condition of affairs later asserted by defendant;
Plaintiff relies on the representation; and
Plaintiff suffers detriment by a change in position as a result of the representation and reliance thereon.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)

Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(p), Fla. Stat. (four years) (Florida courts have not addressed the applicable statute of limitations for estoppel claims). (3) Equitable estoppel requires proof of fraud, misrepresentation or deception. See [Lennar Homes v. Gabb Const. Services, 654 So. 2d 649, 652 (Fla. 3d DCA 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2555388751010948613). (4) The promisee had knowledge of, or reasonable ability to learn, the true facts. See [Irvine v. Cargill Investor Servs., Inc., 799 F.2d 1461, 1463 (11th Cir. 1986)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16878487066174415071); Proccor Pharm., Inc. v. World Health Products, LLC, No. 8:22-CV-2227-SDM-SPF, 2024 WL 3758013, at *23 (M.D. Fla. July 3, 2024). (5) The representation must be definite and specific, and not susceptible to multiple interpretations. See [Irvine v. Cargill Investor Servs., Inc., 799 F.2d 1461, 1463 (11th Cir. 1986)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16878487066174415071). (6) Courts may only employ equitable estoppel to prohibit the perpetration of fraud. See [Lennar Homes v. Gabb Const. Servs., 654 So. 2d 649, 651 (Fla. 3d DCA 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2555388751010948613). (7) The promisee cannot base an estoppel claim against the state for mistaken statements of law. See [Warren v. Dept. of Admin., 554 So. 2d 568, 571 n.1 (Fla. 5th DCA 1989)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17061122550972655576). (8) Estoppel is not a judicial counteraction to the statute of frauds. [Bergman v. DeIulio, 826 So.2d 500, 504 (Fla. 4th DCA 2002)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8121773227184818308)(citations omitted). (9) “[A] truthful statement as to the present intention of a party with regard to his future act is not the foundation upon which an estoppel may be built.” [S. Inv. Corp. v. Norton, 57 So.2d 1, 3 (Fla.1952)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7690981299524179079). (10) A claim of reliance must fail where both parties have equal knowledge of the truth. [Watson Clinic, LLP v. Verzosa, 816 So.2d 832 , 834 (Fla. 2nd DCA 2002)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6367056373834793529)

Under Florida law, equitable estoppel is not an independent cause of action and cannot be brought as a stand-alone claim. Millennium Funding, Inc. v. 1701 Mgmt. LLC, 2021 WL 5882999, *17 (S.D. Fla. Dec. 13, 2021).

title: False Imprisonment
description: False imprisonment is identical to false arrest. [Card v. Miami Dade County Florida, 147 F. Supp. 2d 1334, 1347 (S.D. Fla. 2001)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11705428443503201061). Courts use the terms “confine” and “restrain” interchangeably in defining the elements of false imprisonment. See [Maybin v. Thompson, 606 So. 2d 1240, 1242 (Fla. 2d DCA 1992)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6789914816083669285).
elements: Defendant intended to confine the plaintiff;
Defendant performed an act resulting in plaintiff’s confinement; and
Plaintiff was conscious of the confinement or resulting harm.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(o), Fla. Stat. (four years); [Ervans v. City of Venice, 169 So.3d 267, 268 (Fla. 2d DCA 2015)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17922610984381071166).

Imprisonment pursuant to valid legal process, such as an arrest warrant, cannot support a claim for false imprisonment. Johnson v. Weiner, 155 Fla. 169, 19 So. 2d 699, 700 (1944); Hall v. Dawson, 2016 WL 5853744, at *9 (N.D. Fla. September 1, 2016) (holding “the general rule is that arrest and imprisonment, if based upon a facially valid process, cannot be false”). See also [Jones v. State, 302 So.3d 414, 415 (Fla. 2d DCA 2019).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10280131911148270478)

Plaintiff may not bring claim for false imprisonment where a police officer had probable cause to confine the plaintiff. [Rivero v. Howard, 218 So.3d 992, 994 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&as_sdt=40006&q=rivero+v+howard&btnG=); [Hendricks v. Sheriff, 492 Fed.Appx. 90, 94-95 (11th Cir. 2012)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2696676852447623056); [Ford v. City of Boynton Beach, 323 So.3d 215, 219 (Fla. 4th DCA 2021)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3017689550211061068). Under the any-crime rule, officers are also immune to claims of false-arrest whenever probable cause existed to arrest the plaintiff for any crime, even if that crime was not what the officer thought had occurred. [Scott v. City of Miami](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3894364775857610015), No. 23-11280, 2025 WL 1647025, at *8 (11th Cir. June 11, 2025). Additionally, the mere fact that an officer may have acted without probable cause is not enough to bring a claim, a plaintiff must show the officer acted in bad faith, and under Florida law, “an agent can commit a wrongful, and even intentional, act and still lack bad faith.” [Eiras v. Florida, 239 F.Supp.3d 1331, 1334 (M.D. Fla. 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16742962731036476703).

Private citizens are not liable for false imprisonment resulting from mistakenly reporting an incident to the police that results in the alleged actor’s imprisonment where the citizen made such report in good faith. [Pokorny v. First Fed. Sav. & Loan Ass’n of Largo, 382 So. 2d 678, 682 (Fla. 1980)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18127585724281174315).

title: Florida Consumer Collection Practices Act
description: The elements of an FCCPA claim are nearly identical to the elements of a Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (“FDCPA”) claim. The first prong is substantially identical to the FDCPA, as the FCCPA only applies to consumer debt. The second prong differs from the FDCPA in that the FCCPA prohibits the acts of “persons” and, accordingly, is not limited to “debt collectors.” The third prong requires an act or omission prohibited by the FCCPA. In addition to these elements, several subsections of §559.72 require an allegation of knowledge or intent by the defendant in order to state a cause of action. [Deutsche Bank Nat. Tr. Co. v. Foxx](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6241989678901573154), 971 F. Supp. 2d 1106, 1114 (M.D. Fla. 2013); see also Helman v. Bank of Am., 685 F. App’x 723, 726–27 (11th Cir. 2017) (“The FCCPA applies to anyone who attempts to collect a consumer debt . . . unlike the FDCPA . . . .”); [Crawford v. LVNV Funding, LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15631228362360253615), 758 F.3d 1254, 1258 n.3 (11th Cir. 2014) (“[T]he FDCPA does not apply to all creditors; it applies only to professional debt-collectors . . . .”).
elements: The plaintiff has been the object of collection activity arising from a consumer debt;
The defendant is a person attempting to collect the consumer debt; and
The defendant has engaged in an act or omission prohibited by the FCCPA.
defenses: [Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: Within two years after the date the alleged violation occurred. Fla. Stat. § 559.77(4).

A person may not be held liable in any action brought under this section if the person shows by a preponderance of the evidence that the violation was not intentional and resulted from a bona fide error, notwithstanding the maintenance of procedures reasonably adapted to avoid such error. [Babani v. Broward Auto](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12073160035912816188), 348 So. 3d 608, 610 (Fla. 4th DCA 2022).

The statute provides that in applying and construing this section, due consideration and great weight shall be given to the interpretations of the Federal Trade Commission and the federal courts relating to the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (“FDCPA”). Fla. Stat. §559.77(4); e.g., Schulte v. Newrez LLC, 2023 WL 6407601, at *7 (S.D. Fla. Sept. 1, 2023); [Harb v. Westlake Services LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3108830743420232729), 748 F. Supp. 3d 1170, 1188 (M.D. Fla. 2024).

For FCCPA to apply to a transaction, the obligation must meet the definition of “debt” under section 559.55(6), which states: “‘Debt’ or ‘consumer debt’ means any obligation or alleged obligation of a consumer to pay money arising out of a transaction in which money, property, insurance, or services which are the subject of the transaction are primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, whether or not such obligation has been reduced to judgment.” Fla. Stat § 559.77(6); e.g., [Korkmas v. Onyx Creative Grp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16954466705258090432), 298 So. 3d 690, 692 (Fla. 1st DCA 2020).

A claim under section 559.72(5) has three elements: (1) there was a disclosure of information to a person other than a member of plaintiff’s family; (2) the person did not have a legitimate business need for the information; and (3) the information affected plaintiff’s reputation. Fla. Stat. § 559.72(5); [Heard v. Mathis](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4694730625446248123), 344 So. 2d 651, 655 (Fla. 1st DCA 1977).

A claim under section 559.72(9) has three elements: “an illegitimate debt, a threat or attempt to enforce that debt, and knowledge that the debt is illegitimate.” [Davis v. Sheridan Healthcare Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5158568034450772715), 281 So. 3d 1259, 1264 (Fla. 2d DCA 2019)

Any person who fails to comply with any provision of s. 559.72 is liable for actual damages and for additional statutory damages as the court may allow, but not exceeding $1,000, together with court costs and reasonable attorney’s fees incurred by the plaintiff. In determining the defendant’s liability for any additional statutory damages, the court shall consider the nature of the defendant’s noncompliance with s. 559.72, the frequency and persistence of the noncompliance, and the extent to which the noncompliance was intentional. Fla. Stat. §559.77(2).

A court may award punitive damages if the plaintiff can establish malicious intent. Fla. Stat. §559.77(2); e.g., [Tallahassee Title Co. v. Dean](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=696644312600466787), 411 So. 2d 204, 205 (Fla. 1st DCA 1982).
A court may provide such equitable relief as if deems necessary or proper, including enjoining the defendant from further violations of the FCCPA. Fla. Stat. §559.77(3).

In a class action lawsuit brought under this section the court may award additional statutory damages of up to $1,000 for each named plaintiff and an aggregate award of additional statutory damages of up to the lesser of $500,000 or 1 percent of the defendant’s net worth for all remaining class members; however, the aggregate award may not provide an individual class member with additional statutory damages in excess of $1,000. Fla. Stat. §559.77(3).

title: Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act
description: [Fla. Stat. Ch. 501](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0500-0599/0501/0501PARTIIContentsIndex.html)
elements: A deceptive act or unfair practice;
Causation; and
Actual damages.
defenses: [Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: Fla. Stat. § 95.11(3) (four years).

An unfair practice has been defined as “one that offends established public policy and one that is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous or substantially injurious to consumers.” [PNR, Inc. v. Beacon Prop. Mgmt., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16302029218670515068), 842 So. 2d 773, 777 (Fla. 2003).

An act need not violate a specific rule or regulation to be considered deceptive under FDUTPA. [State v. Tenet Healthcare Corp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7795451224679227976), 420 F. Supp. 2d 1288 (S.D. Fla. 2005).
FDUPTA does not cover “act[s] or practice[s] required or specifically permitted by federal or state law.” Section 501.211(2), Fla. Stat.

Damages, fees, or costs are not recoverable under Section 501.211(2), Fla. Stat. against a retailer who has, in good faith, engaged in the dissemination of claims of a manufacturer or wholesaler without actual knowledge that it violated this section.
Although FDUTPA does not explicitly define the term “deception,” the provisions of the Act are to be “construed liberally.” Section 501.202, Fla. Stat.

Courts have determined that a deceptive practice occurs when there is “a representation, omission, or practice that is likely to mislead the consumer acting reasonably in the circumstances, to the consumer’s detriment.” [Nuwer v. FCA U.S. LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13063360527573755854), 2023 WL 8698327, at *4–5 (S.D. Fla. Dec. 15, 2023) (quoting [PNR, Inc. v. Beacon Prop. Mgmt., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16302029218670515068), 842 So. 2d 773, 777 (Fla. 2003); [Gov't Employees Ins. Co. v. Right Spinal Clinic, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7443088606526880266), No. 23-11778, 2024 WL 4564168, at *9 (11th Cir. Oct. 24, 2024)

Because the courts employ an objective test to determine whether the practice was likely to deceive a consumer acting reasonably, “[a] party asserting a deceptive trade practice claim need not show actual reliance on the representation or omission at issue.” [Carriuolo v. GM Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14880548223775968420), 823 FF.3d 977, 984 (11th Cir. 2016) (quoting [Davis v. Powertel, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5096443149133845156), 776 So. 2d 971, 973 (Fla. 1st DCA 2000)).

In FDUTPA claims, “actual damages” have long been defined as “the difference in the market value of the product or service in the condition in which it was delivered and its market value in the condition in which it should have been delivered according to the contract of the parties.” E.g., [Ounjian v. Globoforce, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1747678145472193267), 89 F.4th 852, 860-61 (11th Cir. 2023) (quoting [Rollins, Inc. v. Heller](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1304778883286458931), 454 So. 2d 580, 585 (Fla. 3d DCA 1984)).

Consequential damages are not available under FDUPTA. E.g., [City First Mortg. Corp. v. Barton](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13802610153250322485), 988 So. 2d 82, 86 (Fla. 4th DCA 2008) (indicating consequential or special damages are not recoverable as “actual damages” under FDUTPA).

“To state a claim for equitable relief, an entity must show: (1) that it is aggrieved, the injury claimed to have been, are being, or will be adversely affected, by (2) a violation of FDUTPA, meaning an unfair or deceptive practice which is injurious to consumers. Further, ‘for someone to be aggrieved, the injury claimed to have been suffered cannot be merely speculative.’” [Stewart Agency, Inc. v. Arrigo Enters.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11248920904352249593), 266 So. 3d 207, 214 (Fla. 4th DCA 2019).

“FDUTPA applies to private causes of action arising from single unfair or deceptive acts in the conduct of any trade or commerce, even if it involves only a single party, a single transaction, or a single contract.” [PNR, Inc. v. Beacon Prop. Mgmt., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16302029218670515068), 842 So. 2d 773, 777 (Fla. 2003).

“To the extent an action giving rise to a breach of contract or breach of lease may also constitute an unfair or deceptive act, such a claim is and has always been cognizable under the FDUTPA.” [PNR, Inc. v. Beacon Prop. Mgmt., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16302029218670515068), 842 So. 2d 773, 777 n.2 (Fla. 2003).

FDUTPA is not applicable to cause of action alleging trademark infringement. [Babbit Electronics, Inc. v. Dynascan Corp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2419982464658986634), 38 F.3d 1161, 1182 n.7 (11th Cir. 1994).

Arbitration clauses have repeatedly been held to apply to statutory claims, including FDUTPA. See, e.g., [Great W. Fin. Sec., Corp. v. Grandison](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14861777224483755310), 701 So. 2d 1202 (Fla. 5th DCA 1997) (reversing the trial court’s order denying appellants’ motion to compel arbitration of statutory civil theft claim).

FDUTPA applies to non-Florida residents if the offending conduct took place predominately or entirely in Florida. [Felice v. Invicta Watch Co. of Am., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6488969607698604749), 2017 WL 3336715, at *2–3 (S.D. Fla. Aug. 4, 2017).

An uninsured patient’s allegations that she paid approximately six times what it cost a hospital to treat her was sufficient for unreasonable pricing claim against the hospital under FDUTPA. [Colomar v. Mercy Hosp., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7288844944178873899), 461 F. Supp. 2d (S.D. Fla. 2006).

title: Forcible Entry and Detention
description: Florida Athletic & Health Club v. Royce, 33 So. 2d 222, 224 (Fla. 1948); [Fla. Stat. Ch. 82](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0000-0099/0082/0082ContentsIndex.html).
elements: Plaintiff was in possession of real property;
Plaintiff was ousted of actual possession of the property; and
Defendant withheld possession of the property from Plaintiff without their consent.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: §95.11(3), Fla. Stat. (four years).
The person entitled to possession is not required to notify the prospective defendant before filing the action. §82.03(1).

If the court finds that the entry or detention by the defendant is willful and knowingly wrongful, the court must award the plaintiff damages equal to double the reasonable rental value of the real property from the beginning of the forcible entry, unlawful entry, or unlawful detention until possession is delivered to the plaintiff. The plaintiff may also recover other damages, including, but not limited to, damages for waste. §82.03(2).
Actions for possession and damages may be bifurcated. §82.03(3); Estate 8, LLC v. Carrington Mortg. Servs. LLC, 2021 WL 3934171, at *2 (S.D. Fla. Apr. 15, 2021).

All actions under this chapter must be brought by summary procedure as provided in Section 51.011, Fla. Stat., and the court shall advance the cause on the calendar. §82.03(4); e.g., [Crocker v. Diland Corp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3848427087390887534), 593 So. 2d 1096, 1098 (Fla. 5th DCA 1992).

It is immaterial whether plaintiff had the legal right of possession to the subject property when ousted; “[s]o long as [plaintiff] had peaceful prior possession and had been forcibly put out of that possession by defendant, the action would lie.” [Floro v. Parker](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1131868992841227087), 205 So. 2d 363, 366 (Fla. 2d DCA 1967).

“Unlawful entry” is applicable where the entry is without force but without due process of law and without the consent of the party in possession, and “forcible entry” is applicable where the entry is accompanied by force or with a multitude of people. Fla. Athletic & Health Club v. Royce, 33 So. 2d 222, 225 (Fla. 1948).

An unlawful detainer action in Florida concerns only the right of possession and any damages, not questions of title. E.g., [CSC Serviceworks, Inc. v. Boca Bayou Condo. Ass’n](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2923199911056192688), 240 So. 3d 12, 14 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018).

title: Fraud
description: “Justifiable reliance is not a necessary element of fraudulent misrepresentation.” [Butler v. Yusem, 44 So. 3d 102, 105 (Fla. 2010)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5280027566079931596)(emphasis added).
elements: Defendant made a false statement regarding a material fact;
Defendant knew or should have known the representation was false;
Defendant intended that the representation induce plaintiff to act on it; and
Plaintiff suffered damages in justifiable reliance on the representation.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(j), Fla. Stat. (four years); [Dixon v. Green Tree Servicing, LLC, No. 19-80022-CIV-MARRA/MATTHEWMAN, 2019 WL 2866495, at *10 (S.D. Fla. July 3, 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16652641049483189205).

The statute of repose provides that a claim for fraud must be commenced “within 12 years after the date of the commission of the alleged fraud, regardless of the date the fraud was or should have been discovered”. See § 95.031(2)(a), Fla. Stat.; [Philip Morris USA Inc. v. Gentile, 281 So.3d 493, 494 n. 2 (Fla. 4th DCA 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=541813019853744951); [Dixon v. Green Tree Servicing, LLC, No. 19-80022-CIV-MARRA/MATTHEWMAN, 2019 WL 2866495, at *10 (S.D. Fla. July 3, 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16652641049483189205).

Mere opinions or misrepresentations of law are not actionable. See e.g., [Bailey v. Trenman, Simmons, Kemker, Scharf, Barkin, Frye & O’Neil, 938 F. Supp. 825, 829 (S.D. Fla. 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4583380040657990380); [MDVIP, Inc. v. Beber, 222 So.3d 555, 561 (Fla. 4th DCA 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9496242344965114163).

False statements regarding promised future action are not actionable unless the promisor had no intentions of performance at the time of the representation. See [Thor Bear, Inc v. Crocker Mizner Park, Inc., 648 So. 2d 168, 172 (Fla. 4th DCA 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11303536794207363198); [940 Lincoln Road Assocs. LLC v. 940 Lincoln Road Enterps. Inc., 237 So.3d 1099, 1102 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13776249107509127588). (6) Reliance on misrepresentations are unreasonable where the statements are contained in a subsequent written agreement between the parties. See [Barnes v. Burger King Corp., 932 F. Supp. 1420, 1427 (S.D. Fla. 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9270473327506925189); Fin-S Tech, LLC v. Surf Hardware International-USA, Inc., No. 13-CV-80645, 2014 WL 12461349, at *8 (S.D. Fla. Jan. 8, 2014); [Ferox, LLC v. ConSeal Int’l, Inc., 175 F.Supp.3d 1363, 1376 (S.D. Fla. 2016)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6623958747207980747). (7) Waiver is a defense to fraud when the allegedly defrauded party had actual or imputed knowledge of the facts supporting the fraud claim. See [Coral Gables Imported Motorcars, Inc. v. Fiat Motors of North America, Inc., 673 F.2d 1234, 1240 (11th Cir. 1982), cert. denied, 459 U.S. 1104 (1983)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17307012481025349289); BGW Design Ltd., Inc. v. Service America Corp., No. 10-20730-Civ, 2011 WL 13220382, at *10 (S.D. Fla. Nov. 30, 2011). (8) Fraudulent misrepresentations do not result from a seller’s puffery in stating opinions or commendations about a product’s value. See [Wasser v. Sasoni, 652 So. 2d 411, 412 (Fla. 3d DCA 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6973888295192539848); [Baker v. Brunswick Corp., No. 2:17–cv–572–FtM–99MRM, 2018 WL 1947433, at *7 (M.D. Fla. April 25, 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12111589288729385995). (9) Under the Independent Tort Doctrine, “It is a fundamental, long-standing common law principle that a plaintiff may not recover in tort for a contract dispute unless the tort is independent of any breach of contract.” [Island Travel & Tours, Ltd., Co. v. MYR Independent, Inc., 300 So.3d 1236, 1239 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11867908773865061540) citing [Peebles v. Puig, 223 So.3d 1065, 1068 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2854220464232358926); [Med-Stop, Inc. v. Vandutch, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3244597855229854791), No. 23-CV-21875, 2025 WL 26731, at *4-5 (S.D. Fla. Jan. 3, 2025).

To assert the defense of fraud, the party must allege with specificity the relevant facts and circumstances supporting the defense, as well as all of the essential elements of fraudulent conduct. [Zikofsky v. Robby Vapor Systems, Inc., 846 So.2d 684, 685 (Fla. 4th DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16097539847842959164); [Meridian Trust Co. v. Batista, No. 17-23051-WILLIAMS, 2018 WL 4760277, at *3 (S.D. Fla. Sept. 30, 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10688345433808725868).

A party cannot recover for fraudulent oral representations which are covered in or contradicted by a later written agreement. [Philip Morris USA Inc. v. Gentile, 281 So.3d 493, 496 (Fla. 4th DCA 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=541813019853744951); Fin-S Tech, LLC v. Surf Hardware International-USA, Inc., No. 13-CV-80645, 2014 WL 12461349, at *8 (S.D. Fla. Jan. 8, 2014); [Giallo v. New Piper Aircraft, Inc., 855 So.2d 1273, 1275 (Fla. 4th DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9880075136308243673).

“If the [allegedly fraudulent] statements are ‘likely to mislead reasonable consumers,’ then it makes no difference if the statements are ‘technically or literally true.’” [Zamber v. American Airlines Inc., 282 F.Supp.3d 1289, 1299 (S.D. Fla. 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13188658014337319416)(citation omitted).

A plaintiff may assert a claim for fraud and breach of contract where the claim for fraudulent inducement is based on facts separate and distinct from the breach of contract claim and such tort (e.g., a species of fraud or negligent misrepresentation) is committed independently of the breach of contract. E.g., [Tiara Condominium Assoc.’n, Inc. v. Marsh & McLennan Companies, Inc., 110 So.3d 399, 402-403 (Fla. 2013)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2579241066312764846).

“[W]hile ‘an express waiver of the right to maintain a fraud claim is all that is required to avoid liability for fraud,’ more than a mere disclaiming of the making of fraudulent representations or a reliance thereon is required to effectuate such a waiver; rather, the parties must agree that ‘even if a fraud “may have been committed,” such a claim may not be asserted.’”[NM Residential, LLC v. Prospect Park Dev., LLC, 2022 WL 880594, *1 (Fla. 2d DCA Mar. 25, 2022)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11780802223386054911)(quoting Billington v. Ginn-La Pine Island, Ltd., 192 So. 3d 77, 84 (Fla. 5th DCA 2016) (quoting Oceanic Villas, Inc. v. Godson, 4 So. 2d 689, 691 (1941))).

description: The elements of claims for fraud in the inducement, fraud in the performance, fraudulent misrepresentation and negligent misrepresentation are identical and differ only by the underlying facts supporting each claim. Compare [Pulte Home Corp. v. Osmose Wood Preserving, Inc., 60 F.3d 734, 742 (11th Cir. 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=673706185954035668)(fraud in the inducement), with [Baggett v. Electricians Credit Union, 620 So. 2d 784, 786 (Fla. 2d DCA 1993)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15754698138090709919)(negligent misrepresentation), and [Johnson v. Davis, 480 So. 2d 625, 627 (Fla. 1985)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14586619263907958570)(fraudulent misrepresentation). [Yamashita v. Merck & Co., 2012 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 17890 (S.D. Fla. February 13, 2012)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12823824079799971662). Fraud is also known as the tort of deceit. See [Crown Eurocars, Inc. v. Schropp, 636 So. 2d 30, 37 (Fla. 2d DCA 1993), aff’d, 654 So. 2d 1158 (Fla. 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12823824079799971662).
elements: Defendant made a false statement regarding a material fact;
Defendant knew or should have known the representation was false;
Defendant intended that the representation induce plaintiff to act on it; and
Plaintiff suffered damages in justifiable reliance on the representation.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(j), Fla. Stat. (four years). (3) The statute of repose provides that a claim for fraud must be commenced “within 12 years after the date of the commission of the alleged fraud, regardless of the date the fraud was or should have been discovered”. See § 95.031(2)(a), Fla. Stat.

Mere opinions or misrepresentations of law are not actionable. See e.g., [Bailey v. Trenman, Simmons, Kemker, Scharf, Barkin, Frye & O’Neil, 938 F. Supp. 825, 829 (S.D. Fla. 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4583380040657990380); [MDVIP, Inc. v. Beber, 222 So.3d 555, 561 (Fla. 4th DCA 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9496242344965114163).

False statements regarding promised future action are not actionable unless the promisor had no intentions of performance at the time of the representation. See [Thor Bear, Inc v. Crocker Mizner Park, Inc., 648 So. 2d 168, 172 (Fla. 4th DCA 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11303536794207363198). (6) Reliance on misrepresentations are unreasonable where the statements are contained in a subsequent written agreement between the parties. See [Barnes v. Burger King Corp., 932 F. Supp. 1420, 1427 (S.D. Fla. 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9270473327506925189); Fin-S Tech, LLC v. Surf Hardware International-USA, Inc., No. 13-CV-80645, 2014 WL 12461349, at *8 (S.D. Fla. Jan. 8, 2014); [Ferox, LLC v. ConSeal Int’l, Inc., 175 F.Supp.3d 1363, 1376 (S.D. Fla. 2016)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6623958747207980747). (7) Waiver is a defense to fraud when the allegedly defrauded party had actual or imputed knowledge of the facts supporting the fraud claim. See [Coral Gables Imported Motorcars, Inc. v. Fiat Motors of North America, Inc., 673 F.2d 1234, 1240 (11th Cir. 1982), cert. denied, 459 U.S. 1104 (1983)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17307012481025349289); BGW Design Ltd., Inc. v. Service America Corp., No. 10-20730-Civ, 2011 WL 13220382, at *10 (S.D. Fla. Nov. 30, 2011). (8) Fraudulent misrepresentations do not result from a seller’s puffery in stating opinions or commendations about a product’s value. See [Wasser v. Sasoni, 652 So. 2d 411, 412 (Fla. 3d DCA 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6973888295192539848); [Baker v. Brunswick Corp., No. 2:17–cv–572–FtM–99MRM, 2018 WL 1947433, at *7 (M.D. Fla. April 25, 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12111589288729385995). (9) “It is a fundamental, long-standing common law principle that a plaintiff may not recover in tort for a contract dispute unless the tort is independent of any breach of contract.” [Island Travel & Tours, Ltd., Co. v. MYR Independent, Inc., 300 So.3d 1236, 1239 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020) citing Peebles v. Puig, 223 So.3d 1065, 1068 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11867908773865061540)

To assert the defense of fraud, the party must allege with specificity the relevant facts and circumstances supporting the defense, as well as all of the essential elements of fraudulent conduct. [Zikofsky v. Robby Vapor Systems, Inc., 846 So.2d 684, 685 (Fla. 4th DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16097539847842959164); [Meridian Trust Co. v. Batista, No. 17-23051-WILLIAMS, 2018 WL 4760277, at *3 (S.D. Fla. Sept. 30, 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10688345433808725868).

A party cannot recover for fraudulent oral representations which are covered in or contradicted by a later written agreement. [Giallo v. New Piper Aircraft, Inc., 855 So.2d 1273, 1275 (Fla. 4th DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9880075136308243673); Fin-S Tech, LLC v. Surf Hardware International-USA, Inc., No. 13-CV-80645, 2014 WL 12461349, at *8 (S.D. Fla. Jan. 8, 2014). (12) A plaintiff may assert a claim for fraud and breach of contract where the claim for fraudulent inducement is based on facts separate and distinct from the breach of contract claim and such tort (e.g., a species of fraud or negligent misrepresentation) is committed independently of the breach of contract. Brunswick Corp., No. 2:17–cv–572–FtM–99MRM, 2018 WL 1947433, at *7 (M.D. Fla. April 25, 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12111589288729385995).

“It is a fundamental, long-standing common law principle that a plaintiff may not recover in tort for a contract dispute unless the tort is independent of any breach of contract.” [Island Travel & Tours, Ltd., Co. v. MYR Independent, Inc., 300 So.3d 1236, 1239 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11867908773865061540) citing [Peebles v. Puig, 223 So.3d 1065, 1068 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2854220464232358926)

To assert the defense of fraud, the party must allege with specificity the relevant facts and circumstances supporting the defense, as well as all of the essential elements of fraudulent conduct. [Zikofsky v. Robby Vapor Systems, Inc., 846 So.2d 684, 685 (Fla. 4th DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16097539847842959164); [Meridian Trust Co. v. Batista, No. 17-23051-WILLIAMS, 2018 WL 4760277, at *3 (S.D. Fla. Sept. 30, 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10688345433808725868).

A party cannot recover for fraudulent oral representations which are covered in or contradicted by a later written agreement. [Philip Morris USA Inc. v. Gentile, 281 So.3d 493, 496 (Fla. 4th DCA 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=541813019853744951); Fin-S Tech, LLC v. Surf Hardware International-USA, Inc., No. 13-CV-80645, 2014 WL 12461349, at *8 (S.D. Fla. Jan. 8, 2014); [Giallo v. New Piper Aircraft, Inc., 855 So.2d 1273, 1275 (Fla. 4th DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9880075136308243673).

“If the [allegedly fraudulent] statements are ‘likely to mislead reasonable consumers,’ then it makes no difference if the statements are ‘technically or literally true.’” [Zamber v. American Airlines Inc., 282 F.Supp.3d 1289, 1299 (S.D. Fla. 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13188658014337319416) (citation omitted).

A plaintiff may assert a claim for fraud and breach of contract where the claim for fraudulent inducement is based on facts separate and distinct from the breach of contract claim and such tort (e.g., a species of fraud or negligent misrepresentation) is committed independently of the breach of contract. E.g., [Tiara Condominium Assoc.’n, Inc. v. Marsh & McLennan Companies, Inc., 110 So.3d 399, 402-403 (Fla. 2013)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2579241066312764846).

“[W]hile ‘an express waiver of the right to maintain a fraud claim is all that is required to avoid liability for fraud,’ more than a mere disclaiming of the making of fraudulent representations or a reliance thereon is required to effectuate such a waiver; rather, the parties must agree that ‘even if a fraud “may have been committed,” such a claim may not be asserted.’”[NM Residential, LLC v. Prospect Park Dev., LLC, 2022 WL 880594, *1 (Fla. 2d DCA Mar. 25, 2022)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11780802223386054911) (quoting Billington v. Ginn-La Pine Island, Ltd., 192 So. 3d 77, 84 (Fla. 5th DCA 2016) (quoting Oceanic Villas, Inc. v. Godson, 4 So. 2d 689, 691 (1941)).

title: Fraudulent Nondisclosure with Real Estate Transactions
description: Very few courts outline the elements of a cause of action for Fraudulent Nondisclosure with Real Estate Transactions. As a result, below you will find those cases that do and those cases that provide a robust discussion of the claim.
elements: The seller of a home must have knowledge of a defect in the property;
The defect must materially affect the value of the property;
The defect must be not readily observable and must be unknown to the buyer; and
The buyer must establish that the seller failed to disclose the defect to the buyer.”
defenses: [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: 95.11(3)(j), Fla. Stat. (four years).

“[T]o hold the seller liable under Johnson, the buyer must prove the seller’s actual knowledge of an undisclosed material defect.” [Eiman v. Sullivan](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16515081383281046202), 173 So. 3d 994, 997 (Fla. 2d DCA 2015) (citing, [Jensen v. Bailey](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4423299370488853901), 76 So.3d 980, 983 (Fla. 2d DCA 2011))(emphasis added).

A Fraudulent Nondisclosure with Real Estate Transactions claim does not apply to commercial transactions. [Futura Realty v. Lone Star Bldg. Ctrs. (E.), Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15042763082471613501), 578 So. 2d 363, 364-65 (Fla. 3d DCA 1991).

To be successful in a Fraudulent Nondisclosure with Real Estate Transactions claim the nondisclosure needs to be of a physical defect present in the property that was sold. [Azam v. M/I Schottenstein Homes, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11856608010846376510), 761 So. 2d 1195, 1196 (Fla. 4th DCA 2000).

The elements of a Fraudulent Nondisclosure with Real Estate Transactions claim do not make the seller of the house a guarantor of the property’s conditions. Is needed evidence that the seller knew of the conditions affecting the house. Brown v. Carter, [13 So. 3d 111](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11084582746183928333), 114 (Fla. 2d DCA 2009); [Slitor v. Elias](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7667432268784458232), 544 So. 2d 255, 258-59 (Fla. 2d DCA 1989).

A Fraudulent Nondisclosure with Real Estate Transactions claim applies only “[t]o sellers, those in privity with the buyer, individuals acting as agents on behalf of the seller (e.g., a real estate broker or closing agent), or those who have a fiduciary or some other special relationship with the buyer.” [Virgilio v. Ryland Grp., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17139370040982207455), 695 F. Supp. 2d 1276, 1283 (M.D. Fla. 2010)(emphasis added).

A buyer may not prevail in a claim when the house conditions “were readily observable and/or within the buyer’s ability to know or easily discover.” [Diaz v. Kosch](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15858296932303262391), 250 So. 3d 156, 166 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018) (citing [Pressman v. Wolf](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1198826018502871043), 732 So. 2d 356, 362 (Fla. 3d DCA 1999))(emphasis added).

“Absent an express agreement, a material misrepresentation or active concealment of a material fact, the seller cannot be held liable for any harm sustained by the buyer or others as the result of a defect existing at the time of the sale.” [Haskell Co. v. Lane Co., Ltd.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2154673596429924252), 612 So. 2d 669, 671 (Fla. 1st DCA 1993)(emphasis added).

title: Gross Negligence – Employee v. Employer
description: Florida’s Workers’ Compensation Act provides immunity to employers and their employees from suits for simple negligence. This immunity does not extend to cases where the injury is caused by an employer’s intentional tort or by a fellow employee’s gross negligence, willful and wanton misconduct or unprovoked physical aggression. § [440.11](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0400-0499/0440/Sections/0440.11.html)(b), Fla. Stat. (2023); [Fred G. Wright, Inc. v. Edwards](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13352202917396268628), 642 So. 2d 808, 809 (Fla. 2d DCA 1994).
elements: Imminent or clear and present danger amounting to a more than normal or usual peril;
Defendant knew of the imminent danger; and
An act or omission that evinces a conscious disregard of the consequences.
defenses: [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(4)(a), Fla. Stat (two years).

Fellow employee’s conduct does not meet the legal standard for gross negligence: “[C]onduct that is so reckless or wanting in care that it constitutes a conscious disregard or indifference to the life, safety, or rights of persons exposed to such conduct.” [Foreman v. Russo, 624 So. 2d 333, 335 (Fla. 4th DCA 1993)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=620562336924156674).

The injury was not caused by Employer’s Intentional tort. Employer must have “deliberately intended to injure the employee,” or engaged in conduct that was “virtually certain to result in injury and deliberately misrepresented the danger to prevent the employee from exercising informed judgment about whether to perform the work.” § [11(b)](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0400-0499/0440/Sections/0440.11.html), Fla. Stat.

If an employee already filed for and received benefits through workers’ compensation, “a subsequent negligence suit is barred.” This principle also applies to suits against a fellow employee. [Ferraro v. Marr, 467 So. 2d 809, 810 (Fla. 2d DCA 1985)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3544258998611588545).

Immunity against suit does not extend to fellow employees “when each is operating in the furtherance of the employer’s business but they are assigned primarily to unrelated works within private or public employment.” [440.11(1)(b)](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0400-0499/0440/Sections/0440.11.html), Fla. Stat.

title: Implied Way of Necessity
description: “[W]here a person has heretofore granted or hereafter grants lands to which there is no accessible right-of way except over her or his land, or has heretofore retained or hereafter retains land which is inaccessible except over the land which the person conveys. In such instances a right-of-way is presumed to have been granted or reserved.” [Hancock v. Tipton](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2192795605011174743), 732 So. 2d 369, 373 (Fla. 2d DCA 1999) (citation omitted).
elements: “[W]here a person has heretofore granted or hereafter grants lands to which there is no accessible right-of way except over her or his land, or has heretofore retained or hereafter retains land which is inaccessible except over the land which the person conveys. In such instances a right-of-way is presumed to have been granted or reserved.”Hancock v. Tipton, 732 So. 2d 369, 373 (Fla. 2d DCA 1999) (citation omitted).
defenses: [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: 95.11(3)(p), Fla. Stat. (four years).

The party claiming the way of necessity has the burden of proving the elements of the claim. [Goldman v. Lustig](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1432631800370164339), 237 So. 3d 381, 385 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018) (citation omitted); [Parham v. Reddick](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9305149291918894859), 537 So. 2d 132, 135 (Fla. 1st DCA 1988) (citation omitted).

“[S]overeign immunity does not bar a claim for a way of necessity pursuant to section 704.01(1), Florida Statutes.” [Gulf Oil Realty Co. v. Dep’t of Transp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8764640390233826187), 685 So. 2d 1032, 1033 (Fla. 5th DCA 1997); [Fla. Water Mgmt. Dist. v. Layton](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16197625662218820441), 402 So. 2d 597, 598-99 (Fla. 2d DCA 1981) (emphasis added).

To be successful, the claimant must also prove “absolute necessity.” [Goldman v. Lustig](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1432631800370164339), 237 So. 3d 381, 385 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018); [Palm Beach Polo Holdings, Inc. v. Equestrian Club Ests. Prop. Owners Ass’n, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4230131105083578530), 949 So. 2d 347, 349-50 (Fla. 4th DCA 2007)(emphasis added).

The claimant must show that he or she lost access to a public road that existed when the property was acquired. [PGA N. II of Fla., LLC v. Div. of Admin., State of Fla. Dep’t of Transp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7544722870765052310), 126 So. 3d 1150, 1154 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012); [Griffin v. North](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15790687277068439899), 373 So. 2d 96, 97 (Fla. 2d DCA 1979).

“[I]n order for the owner of a dominant tenement to be entitled to a way of necessity over the servient tenement both properties must at one time have been owned by the same party (that is another way of saying that one seeking the grant of a way of necessity must show unity of ownership or common source of title).” [Roy v. Euro-Holland Vastgoed, B. V.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7444060412412979466), 404 So. 2d 410, 412 (Fla. 4th DCA 1981)(emphasis added).

An implied way of necessity can be extinguished by Marketable Record Title Act(MRTA.) [Blanton v. City of Pinellas Park](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1309014200567337458), 887 So. 2d 1224, 1231 (Fla. 2004); [H & F Land, Inc. v. Panama City-Bay Cnty. Airport & Indus. Dist.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15280382777445204389), 736 So. 2d 1167, 1176 (Fla. 1999).

title: Indemnification
description: Indemnification claims may be contractual or equitable in nature. See, e.g., [Allstate Ins. Co. v. Metro. Dade Cty., 436 So.2d 976, 978 (Fla. 3d DCA 1983)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1229973520702271483). In cases involving contractual indemnity, the terms of the agreement will determine whether the indemnitor is obligated to reimburse the indemnitee for a particular claim. Certainly contracts purporting to indemnify a party against its own negligence will only be enforced if they clearly express such an intent and a general provision indemnifying the indemnitee “against any and all claims,” standing alone, is not sufficient. [Camp, Dresser, & Mckee, Inc. v. Paul N. Howard Co., 853 So.2d 1072, 1077 (Fla. 5th DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2936378613531149242).
elements: Plaintiff discharges a duty owed to another party as a result of some vicarious, constructive, derivative or technical liability;
Defendant should have discharged the duty satisfied by Plaintiff;
Plaintiff is without any fault; and
Plaintiff suffered in damages by discharging the liability that should be borne by Defendant.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(p), Fla. Stat. (four years); see also [Dominion of Canada v. State Farm Fire and Casualty Co., 754 So.2d 852, 855 (Fla.2d DCA 2000)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10923296753629927409)(citations omitted). The statute does not begin to run until the Plaintiff discharges the duty owed by the defendant. [E.g., Attorneys’ Title Ins. Fund, Inc. v. Punta Gorda Isles, Inc., 547 So.2d 1250, 1252 (Fla. 2d DCA 1989)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6711816741336083916) (3) A party seeking indemnity must be without fault. [Houdaille Indust., Inc. v. Edwards, 374 So.2d 490, 493 (Fla. 1979)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1052406066918486932); [Florida Peninsula Ins. Co. v. Ken Mullen Plumbing Inc., 171 So.3d 194, 196 (Fla. 5th DCA 2015).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13861059235034588771) (4) An indemnity claim cannot be brought in the absence of a special relationship. See [C.B. Contractors, LLC v. Allens Steel Prod., Inc., 261 So.3d 711, 713 (Fla. 5th DCA 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6044775706765441841)(holding lower court’s conclusion that an indemnity claim was unavailable is incorrect and recognizing a special relationship between contractors and subcontractors for the purposes of indemnification); [Platinum Estates, Inc. v. T.D. Bank, N.A., No. 11–60670–CIV, 2012 WL 760791, at *5 (S.D. Fla. March 8, 2012)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13476190836756520589); [Brickell Biscayne Corp. v. title: Indemnification, Contractual
description: Indemnification claims may be contractual or equitable in nature. See, e.g., [Allstate Ins. Co. v. Metro. Dade Cty., 436 So.2d 976, 978 (Fla. 3d DCA 1983)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1229973520702271483). “In cases involving contractual indemnity, the terms of the agreement will determine whether the indemnitor is obligated to reimburse the indemnitee for a particular claim.” [Camp, Dresser, & Mckee, Inc. v. Paul N. Howard Co., 853 So.2d 1072, 1077 (Fla. 5th DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2936378613531149242). “Certainly contracts purporting to indemnify a party against its own negligence will only be enforced if they clearly express such an intent and a general provision indemnifying the indemnitee “against any and all claims,” standing alone, is not sufficient. [Id.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2936378613531149242)(internal citations omitted).
elements: The party filing the claim cannot be at fault;
The other party must be at fault.
defenses: [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: §95.11(2)(b), Stat. (Five years).

The contract must state in “clear and unequivocal terms” the intention to indemnify a party. [On Target, Inc. v. Allstate Floridian Ins. Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13310218423875799538), 23 So. 3d 180, 183 (Fla. 2d DCA 2009); [Zeiger Crane Rentals, Inc. v. Double A Indus., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8121471075596323734), 16 So. 3d 907, 914 (Fla. 4th DCA 2009).
Claimant must prove that under the terms of the contract he or she is entitled to receive indemnity. Safety Ins. Co. v. GAB Robins N. Am., Inc., 2009 WL 10671231, *4 (M.D. Fla. Jan. 29, 2009).

To indemnify a party against its own wrongful conduct the contract terms must: “express in clear and unequivocal terms an intent to indemnify against the indemnitee’s own wrongful acts; general terms of indemnity will not suffice.” [Welch v. Complete Care Corp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3429437924561028176), 818 So. 2d 645, 650 (Fla. 2d DCA 2002) (citing [Cox Cable Corp. v. Gulf Power Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15686680637570299032), 591 So. 2d 627, 629 (Fla. 1992))(emphasis added).

Consideration must exist to establish an indemnity claim. [Hartford Fire Ins. Co. v. N.Y. Mart Grp., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12197771959734461592), 391 F. Supp. 3d 1175, 1177 (S.D. Fla. June, 21 2019); [Matey v. Pruitt](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14681697961314170140), 510 So. 2d 351, 353 (Fla. 2d DCA 1987).

“Indemnity contracts are subject to the general rules of contractual construction; thus an indemnity contract must be construed based on the intentions of the parties.” [Dade Cnty. Sch. Bd. v. Radio Station WQBA](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11323804062576171249), 731 So. 2d 638, 643 (Fla. 1999)(emphasis added).

“The obligation to indemnify need not be based upon an express contract of indemnification but may arise out of implied contractual relations or out of liability imposed by law.” [Mims Crane Serv., Inc. v. Insley Mfg. Corp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4639863473345783658), 226 So. 2d 836, 839 (Fla. 2d DCA 1969)(emphasis added).

“Generally in Florida, indemnity provisions apply only to third-party claims.” [MVW Mgmt., LLC v. Regalia Beach Devs. LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3153193574716863425), 230 So. 3d 108, 112 (Fla. 3d DCA 2017)(emphasis added).

“When a parent agrees to indemnify the third party for its negligence causing injury to the minor child, the same burden shifting occurs. Indemnification “shifts the entire loss from one … to another who should bear the costs” for damages resulting from tortious activity.” [Claire’s Boutiques v. Locastro](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1265116454086448203), 85 So. 3d 1192, 1198 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012)(citing [Houdaille Indus., Inc. v. Edwards](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1052406066918486932), 374 So. 2d 490, 493 (Fla. 1979))(emphasis added).

In an implied contractual indemnity, “the party alleging a special relationship has a heavy burden of showing an implied agreement by the potential indemnitor to indemnify it.” [Burnett v. A. Bottacchi S.A. de Navegacion](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2518298562392587950), 882 F. Supp. 1050, 1055 (S.D. Fla. Dec. 5, 1994)(emphasis added).

Contractual indemnification provisions must contain “a monetary limitation on the extent of the indemnification that bears a reasonable commercial relationship to the contract.” See S. §725.06(1); see also [Griswold Ready Mix Concrete, Inc. v. Reddick](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9557028101113603164), 134 So.3d 985 (Fla. 1st DCA 2012) (holding that a contractual indemnification provision contained in a construction subcontract agreement between a contractor and a materialman was void and unenforceable pursuant to F.S. §725.06 because it did not contain a dollar limit to the indemnitor’s potential liability).

title: Injunction Permanent
description: It has suffered an irreparable injury; The remedies available at law, such as monetary damages, are inadequate to compensate for that injury; Considering the balance of hardships between the plaintiff and defendant, a remedy in equity is warranted; and The public interest would not be disserved by a permanent injunction.
elements: It has suffered an irreparable injury;
The remedies available at law, such as monetary damages, are inadequate to compensate for that injury;
Considering the balance of hardships between the plaintiff and defendant, a remedy in equity is warranted; and
The public interest would not be disserved by a permanent injunction.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)

Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(p), Fla. Stat. (four years); [Hollywood Lakes Section Civic Ass’n, Inc. v. City of Hollywood, 676 So. 2d 500, 501 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5816033888961628090).

“Mandatory injunctions – [which require that a defendant do some positive act or that acts be undone] – are looked upon with disfavor, and the courts seem even more reluctant to issue them than prohibitory ones.” [Shaw v. Tampa Elec. Co., 949 So.2d 1066, 1070, n.3 (Fla. 2d DCA 2007)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8194209877665634102)(emphasis added); see Antoine ex. rel. I.A. v. School Bd. of Collier Cty., 301 F.Supp.3d 1195, 1202 (M.D. Fla. 2018) (noting that moving party will face a particularly heavy burden of persuasion).

A tenant cannot seek specific performance of a lease against a landlord. E.g., [Cardinal Inv. Group, Inc. v. Giles](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4370495371678261303), 813 So.2d 262, 263 (Fla. 4th DCA 2002).

In addition to satisfaction of prima facie elements, Florida courts must also consider the following in determining whether to grant injunctive relief: “(a) the nature of the interest to be protected, (b) the relative adequacy to the plaintiff of injunction and of other remedies, (c) any unreasonable delay by the plaintiff in bringing suit, (d) any related misconduct on the part of the plaintiff, (e) the relative hardship likely to result to defendant if an injunction is granted and to plaintiff if it is denied, (f) the interests of third persons and of the public, and (g) the practicability of framing and enforcing the order or judgment’’. [Davis v. Joyner, 409 So. 2d 1193, 1195 (Fla. 4th DCA 1982)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3795585124361445338), citing Restatement (Second) of Torts § 936 (1979).

Courts must consider the harm the defendant will suffer by the issuance of an injunction balanced against the harm, if any, the plaintiff may suffer by a denial of an injunction. [Davis v. Joyner, 409 So.2d 1193, 1195 (Fla. 4th DCA 1982)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3795585124361445338); [Sumfinidade Unipessoal LDA v. Yachtlife Techs. Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1216723116565294221), No. 24-CV-21555, 2024 WL 4607072, at *7 (S.D. Fla. Sept. 24, 2024).

A plaintiff with unclean hands may not obtain an injunction. [ABM Fin. Servs., Inc. v. Express Consolidation, Inc., No. 07-60294-CIV, 2008 WL 11403228, at *10 (S.D. Fla. Apr. 18, 2008)](https://1.next.westlaw.com/Document/Ibfb982f01da711e885eba619ffcfa2b1/View/FullText.html?navigationPath=Search%2Fv1%2Fresults%2Fnavigation%2Fi0ad6ad3d0000017301ec017891284d59%3FNav%3DCASE%26fragmentIdentifier%3DIbfb982f01da711e885eba619ffcfa2b1%26parentRank%3D0%26startIndex%3D1%26contextData%3D%2528sc.Search%2529%26transitionType%3DSearchItem&listSource=Search&listPageSource=75eef3bd26852bf6f592a05838721621&list=CASE&rank=3&sessionScopeId=aac83155755e22c0343cf83811b89e5549a540af501734e468af6b37ec24d175&originationContext=Search%20Result&transitionType=SearchItem&contextData=%28sc.Search%29#co_term_6981), report and recommendation adopted, No. 07-60294-CIV, 2008 WL 11403224 (S.D. Fla. May 21, 2008).

Injunctive relief is a remedy and not an independent stand alone cause of action. See, e.g., [Pronman v. Styles, No. 12–80674–CIV, 2015 WL 58629, *11 (S.D. Fla. 2015)(Marra, K.)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5822172964622562350).

A dating violence injunction allows any person “who is the victim of dating violence and has reasonable cause to believe he or she is in imminent danger of becoming the victim of another act of dating violence” may petition the circuit court for an injunction to prevent such violence. [§ 784.046(2)(b), Fla. Stat](https://1.next.westlaw.com/Link/Document/FullText?findType=L&pubNum=1000006&cite=FLSTS784.046&originatingDoc=Idcba4570ec4e11e98c25d953629e1b0a&refType=SP&originationContext=document&transitionType=DocumentItem&contextData=(sc.Search)#co_pp_674e0000c3d66). Dating violence is “any assault, battery, aggravated battery, sexual assault, stalking, aggravated stalking, kidnapping or false imprisonment, or any criminal offense resulting in physical injury or death, by a person against another person” between individuals who have had or currently have a significant, romantic relationship. [§ 784.046(1)(a), (d)](https://1.next.westlaw.com/Link/Document/FullText?findType=L&pubNum=1000006&cite=FLSTS784.046&originatingDoc=Idcba4570ec4e11e98c25d953629e1b0a&refType=SP&originationContext=document&transitionType=DocumentItem&contextData=(sc.Search)#co_pp_9f800000f2221).[Khan v. Deutschman, 282 So.3d 965, 967 (Fla. 1st DCA 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1580382222530560994).

Irreparable harm: “the injury must not be remote or speculative, but actual and imminent . . . In addition to ensuring that injunctive relief was necessary under this standard, the court must also ensure that the scope of the awarded relief does not exceed the identified harm.” [McKinnon v. Hullett, No. 3:18CV1191/LAC/EMT, 2020 WL 1326636, at *12 (N.D. Fla. Feb. 20, 2020)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1183152436025897018)

Abuse of Discretion: The standard for reviewing the denial of a permanent injunction is abuse of discretion. [Hollywood Towers Condo. Ass’n, Inc. v. Hampton, 40 So.3d 784, 786 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17792651717637159264); See [Gulf Bay Land Invs., Inc. v. Trecker, 955 So.2d 1157, 1161 (Fla. 2d DCA 2007)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14507148344945017560).
references:
#### FLORIDA STATE COURTS

“To obtain a temporary injunction, the petitioner must satisfy a four-part test under Florida law: ‘a substantial likelihood of success on the merits; lack of an adequate remedy at law; irreparable harm absent the entry of an injunction; and that injunctive relief will serve the public interest.’ [Liberty Counsel v. Fla. Bar Bd. Of Governors, 12 So. 3d 183, 186 n. 7 (Fla. 2009)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11331864487931420442#[7])(quoting Reform Party of Fla. v. Black, 885 So.2d 303, 305 (Fla. 2004) (citing Dania Jai Alai Int’l, Inc. v. Murua, 375 So.2d 57, 58 (Fla. 4th DCA 1979)). To obtain a permanent injunction, the petitioner must ‘establish a clear legal right, an inadequate remedy at law and that irreparable harm will arise absent injunctive relief.’ [Liberty Counsel, 12 So. 3d 183, at 186 n. 7](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11331864487931420442#[7])(quoting K.W. Brown & Co. v. McCutchen, 819 So.2d 977, 979 (Fla. 4th DCA 2002) (citing Murua, 375 So.2d at 58)). “The standard for issuance of a permanent injunction is essentially the same as that for the issuance of a preliminary injunction, except that a plaintiff seeking the former relief must show actual success on the merits, rather than a mere likelihood of success. [Oliver v. Fuhrman, No. 16-CIV-22053, 2017 WL 6610900, at *8 (S.D. Fla. Oct. 5, 2017)](https://1.next.westlaw.com/Document/Id6ab3320ebc811e7b393b8b5a0417f3d/View/FullText.html?navigationPath=Search%2Fv1%2Fresults%2Fnavigation%2Fi0ad6ad3d0000017301c93fc59128295d%3FNav%3DCASE%26fragmentIdentifier%3DId6ab3320ebc811e7b393b8b5a0417f3d%26parentRank%3D0%26startIndex%3D1%26contextData%3D%2528sc.Search%2529%26transitionType%3DSearchItem&listSource=Search&listPageSource=cee562e74c76df47b0f2b367572b9c53&list=CASE&rank=11&sessionScopeId=aac83155755e22c0343cf83811b89e5549a540af501734e468af6b37ec24d175&originationContext=Search%20Result&transitionType=SearchItem&contextData=%28sc.Search%29#co_term_5198)(citing Klay v. United Healthgroup, Inc., 376 F.3d 1092, 1097 (11th Cir. 2004).

“Under Florida law rulings on an action for a preliminary injunction are generally not considered final or conclusive; the denial of a preliminary injunction does not preclude the subsequent grant of permanent equitable relief . . . the underlying logic is that temporary injunction rulings are generally not conclusive determinations on the merits; they should not bar a more thorough consideration of a claim when the evidence and legal arguments are better developed.” [David Vincent, Inc. v. Broward Cty., Fla., 200 F.3d 1325, 1331 (11th Cir. 2000)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4287520976452135562).

title: Injurious Falsehood
description: Injurious Falsehood is a cause of action akin to defamation. See [Salit v. Ruden, McCloskey, Smith, Schuster & Russell, P.A., 742 So.2d 381, 386-387, n.3 (Fla. 4th DCA 1999)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18043282661782412433); Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 623A-652 (1977).
elements: Defendant made a false and defamatory statement;
Defendant published (written or orally) to a third party;
Defendant made the defamatory statement with the requisite intent (negligence or malice); and
Plaintiff suffered damages.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(4)(g), Fla. Stat. (two years). (3) Truth is an affirmative to defamation claims. When combined with good motive, truth is a complete defense. [Lipsig v. Ramlawi, 760 So. 2d 170, 180 (Fla. 3d DCA 2000)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5632641935110262349); [Turner v. Wells, 198 F. Supp. 3d 1355, 1365 (S.D. Fla. 2016).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3339815892331645363)See also Art. I, § 4, Fla. Const. (4) Statements made during a judicial proceeding are absolutely privileged, provided that such statements are related to the proceeding’s subject matter. See [Levin, Middlebrooks v. U.S. Fire Ins. Co., 639 So.2d 606, 607 (Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16849305990004782225)(absolute privilege extends to parties, witnesses, counsel, and judges). (5) Absolute privilege extends to statements made during labor grievance proceedings, provided that such statements are related to the proceeding’s subject matter. See [Hope v. Nat. Alliance Jacksonville, 320, 649 So.2d 897, 900 (Fla. 1st DCA 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=389824345445520955). (6) Absolute privilege protects statements made by government officials in connection with their official duties. [Hauser v. Urchisin, 231 So.2d 6, 8 (Fla. 1970)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14982816976873030078); [Childrens v. Fla. Gulf Coast Univ. Bd. of Tr., No: 2:15–cv–722–FtM–MRM, 2017 WL 1196575, at *11 (M.D. Fla. Mar. 31, 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12733118467635913136). (7) Qualified privilege protects defamatory statements made by private individuals to the police or the state’s attorney prior to the institution of criminal charges. [Fridovich v. Fridovich, 598 So.2d 65, 69 (Fla. 1992)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2671126229261794235). (8) Qualified privilege protects defamatory statements that are published by a speaker in good faith, pursuant to a duty or special interest, and such privilege is not abused. [Nodar v. Galdbreath, 462 So.2d 803, 809 (Fla. 1984)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11763946123763864156). (9) Statements of pure opinion based on known facts do not give rise to defamation claims. See [Miami Child’s World, Inc. v. Sunbeam Television Corp., 669 So.2d 336, 336 (Fla. 3d DCA 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8428423769510646820); [Turner v. Wells, 198 F. Supp. 3d 1355, 1365 (S.D. Fla. 2016).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3339815892331645363) (10) Minor inconsistencies in news reports are not actionable provided that the report is substantially true and the inaccuracies did not result from deliberate falsification or awareness of probable falsity. [Newton v. Fla. Freedom Newspapers, Inc., 447 So.2d 906, 907 (Fla. 1st DCA 1984)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13897281155145818454). (11) Employers who disclose information about former employees are immune from civil liability if the communication is made in good faith, and such presumption is not rebutted by showing that information “knowingly false or deliberately misleading, was rendered with malicious purpose, or violated any civil right of the former employee protected under chapter 760’’. § 768.095, Fla. Stat. (12) § 770.01, Fla. Stat., requires five (5) days notice to a defendant prior to filing a libel suit. (13) Florida law recognizes the doctrine of defamation by implication, wherein literally true statements can be defamatory where they create a false impression. See [Jews for Jesus, Inc. v. Rapp, 997 SO.2d 1098, 1108 (Fla. 2008)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=187583228716190638)(“[I]f the defendant juxtaposes a series of facts so as to imply a defamatory connection between them, or creates a defamatory implication by omitting facts, he may be held responsible for the defamatory implication, unless it qualifies as an opinion, even though the particular facts are correct.”).

title: Interference with Child Custody
description: [Stone v. Wall](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13790938587237872852), 734 So. 2d 1038, 1041-42 (Fla. 1999).
defenses: [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: 95.11(3)(o), Fla. Stat. (four years).

A claim for interference with child custody cannot be established if the child was taken to prevent physical harm. Brown v. Brown, 800 So. 2d 359, 362 (Fla. 4th DCA 2001) (citing Kessel v. Leavitt, 204 W. Va. 95, 108, 511 S.E.2d 720, 733 (1998)).

A reasonable good faith belief that the interference is proper can release a defendant from liability. [Stone v. Wall](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13790938587237872852), 734 So. 2d 1038, 1042 (Fla. 1999) (citing Kessel v. Leavitt, 204 W. Va. 95, 108, 511 S.E.2d 720, 733 (1998)).

“If there is a violation of a dissolution of marriage order and/or a court approved agreement and/or statutory parental rights, the family court is uniquely positioned to attempt to correct the violation, to minimize harm, and to fashion a remedy, which may include monetary sanctions.” [Davis v. Hilton](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6064304316687971776), 780 So. 2d 974, 976 (Fla. 4th DCA 2001)(emphasis added).

Plaintiff must show he or she had the custody of the child and that the other party interfered with the custody. McIndoo v. Broward Cnty., 750 Fed. Appx. 816, 820 (11th Cir. 2018); [Stone v. Wall](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13790938587237872852), 734 So. 2d 1038, 1042 (Fla. 1999).

title: Invasion of Privacy
description: Appropriation: Unauthorized use of a person’s name or likeness to obtain some benefit. Intrusion: Physically or electronically intruding into one’s private quarters or person. Public Disclosure of Private Facts: Publication of private facts that are offensive to the reasonable person and not of legitimate public concern.
elements: Appropriation:Unauthorized use of a person’s name or likeness to obtain some benefit.
Intrusion:Physically or electronically intruding into one’s private quarters or person.
Public Disclosure of Private Facts:Publication of private facts that are offensive to the reasonable person and not of legitimate public concern.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(a), Fla. Stat. (four years). (3) Express consent to publication is a defense. See [Rawls v. Conde Nast Publications, Inc., 446 F.2d 313, 316-317 (5th Cir. 1971), cert. denied, 404 U.S. 1038 (1972)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=189931746753526073). (4) Implied consent to publication is a defense. See [Florida Pub. Co. v. Fletcher, 340 So.2d 914, 917 (Fla. 1976), cert. denied, 431 U.S. 930 (1977)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9745236850461910908). (5) Plaintiff failed to prove that publication was offensive to the reasonable person. [Harms v. Miami Daily News, Inc., 127 So.2d 715, 718 (Fla. 3d DCA 1961)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15342861923197637009). (6) Public identification is a prerequisite to invasion of privacy claims. See [Epic Metals Corp., v. Condec, Inc., 867 F. Supp. 1009, 1017 (M.D. Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2496243974630663965). (7) Publication of facts of public concern do not give rise to invasion of privacy claim. See [Woodward v. Sunbeam Television Corp., 616 So.2d 501, 503 (Fla. 1993)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7206755349209211866). (8) Disclosure of facts regarding a criminal case obtained from public documents does not give rise to claim for invasion of privacy. See [Cape Publications, Inc. v. Hitchner, 549 So.2d 1374, 1379 (Fla. 1989)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11428914153124448146). (9) Photograph taken in a public place does not give rise to claim for invasion of privacy. See [Heath v. Playboy Enterprises, Inc., 732 F. Supp. 1145, 1148 (S.D. Fla. 1990)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16674309084537690731). (10) Disclosure of facts obtained from public records or proceedings do not give rise to invasion of privacy claim. See [Heath v. Playboy Enterprises, Inc., 732 F. Supp. 1145, 1148 (S.D. Fla. 1990)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16674309084537690731). (11) Invasion of privacy claims, with the exception of appropriation, can be asserted only by the individual whose privacy has been invaded. See [Loft v. Fuller, 408 So.2d 619, 623 (Fla. 4th DCA 1981), reh’ g denied, 419 So.2d 1198 (Fla. 1982)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15300621820639118065). (12) The fair reporting privilege is a defense to claims for invasion of privacy where a broadcast is a “reasonably accurate and fair” description of the contents of information contained in public records. [Woodard v. Sunbeam Television Corp., 616 So.2d 501, 502 (Fla. 3d DCA 1993)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7206755349209211866). (13) The right to privacy does not prohibit the publication of matter which is of legitimate public concern. [Walker v. Florida Dept. of L. Enf’t, 845 So.2d 339, 340 (Fla. 3d DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5645325012521345049); [Jews For Jesus, Inc. v. Rapp, 997 So.2d 1098, 1104 (Fla. 2008).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=187583228716190638) (14) False Light Invasion of Privacy is not a recognized cause of action in the state of Florida. See [Anderson v. Gannett Co., 994 So.2d 1048, 1051 (Fla. 2008)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2363397886093748478); See also [Jews for Jesus, Inc. v. Rapp, 997 So.2d 1098, 1114-15 (Fla. 2008)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=187583228716190638); Harrington v. Veritext, LLC, No. 24-CV-22787, 2025 WL 1591614, at *9-10 (S.D. Fla. May 1, 2025); [Faller v. Beasley Broad. Group, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5538730962540352141), No. 2:24-CV-606-SPC-KCD, 2025 WL 589231, at *2 (M.D. Fla. Feb. 24, 2025). (15) Florida law explicitly requires an intrusion into a private place and not merely into a private activity. See [Celestine v. Capital One, 2017 WL 2838185, at *3 (S.D. Fla. June 30, 2017).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10366341803682447943) (16) In Florida, except in cases of physical invasion, the tort of invasion of privacy must be accompanied by publication to the public in general or to a large number of persons. See [Kautz v. Residence Inn by Marriott, LLC, 2014 WL 4416012, *3 (M.D. Fla. Sept. 5, 2014).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14579959046157485869)
