title: Quiet Title
description: The Plaintiff has title to the property, A cloud exists, and The plaintiff’s title is valid, and the cloud is invalid.
elements: The Plaintiff has title to the property,
A cloud exists, and
The plaintiff’s title is valid, and the cloud is invalid.
defenses: [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations:
28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g) (twelve years) for real property quiet title actions. Wilkins v. United States, 143 S. Ct. 870, 879 (2023).

§ 95.11(2)(c), Fla. Stat. (five years), [mortgage cases. Bank of Am., N.A. v. Graybush](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1675880221004629978), 253 So. 3d 1188, 1191 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018); [Admiral Sec. & Inv. Co. v. Curtis](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1164313438700595041), 804 So. 2d 354, 354 (Fla. 4th DCA 2001).

§ 95.11(3)(j), Fla. Stat. (four years), actions related to fraud. Harriott v. J.P Morgan Chase, 2013 WL 12383296, *1 (S.D. Fla. Aug. 28, 2013); [Padron Warehouse Corp. v. Realty Assocs. Fund III](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17435209448914620385), L.P., 377 F. Supp. 2d 1259, 1269 (S.D. Fla. 2005).
§ 95.12, Fla. Stat. (seven years), for recovery of real property. Harriott v. J.P Morgan Chase, 2013 WL 12383296, *1 (S.D. Fla. Aug. 28, 2013).

§ 95.231, Fla. Stat. (twenty years), Limitations where deed or will on record. Harriott v. J.P Morgan Chase, 2013 WL 12383296, *1 (S.D. Fla. Aug. 28, 2013); [Rigby v. Liles](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17980391631576782841), 505 So. 2d 598, 601 (Fla. 1st DCA 1987).

The claimant must provide sufficient plausible allegations to maintain the quiet title claim. Ebsco Gulf Coast Dev., Inc. v. Salas, 2016 WL 11189984, *6 (N.D. Fla. Sept. 29, 2016); [Stark v. Frayer](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13081791443993841339), 67 So. 2d 237, 239 (Fla. 1953).

The party seeking quiet tittle has the burden of proving the elements of the claim. [Fitzgerald v. Regions Bank](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4078125968931001580), 2013 WL 2371216, *3 (M.D. Fla. May 30, 2013); [Lehrer v. Regions Bank](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4221868001266328245), 2013 WL 2371192, *3 (M.D. Fla. May 30, 2013).

To bring a claim under the Quiet Title Act, the party must prove that there is a problem “concerning the quality of title between the plaintiff and the United States.” [Grames v. Sarasota Cnty.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1661421641435802539), 2021 WL 82847, *3 (M.D. Fla. Jan. 11, 2021) (citing McMaster v. United States, 177 F.3d 936, 939 (11th Cir. 1999))(emphasis added).

A person receiving property from an individual with mental health issues can claim quiet title if the property was obtained through the individual’s legal guardian. [Grigg v. Gatt](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16148571350351210810), 283 So. 2d 369, 370 (Fla. 1st DCA 1973).

“As a general rule boundary line disputes should not be settled by equitable proceedings to quiet title.” [Brown v. Semple](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=730338818208342432), 204 So. 2d 229, 231 (Fla. 3d DCA 1967); [Stark v. Frayer](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13081791443993841339), 67 So. 2d 237, 239 (Fla. 1953)(emphasis added).

The plaintiff must prove that the title to the property is in himself; otherwise, the court of equity will not have jurisdiction over the quiet title claim. [Contreras v. Aurora Loan Servs. LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5357936299772639525), 2017 WL 2669893, *3 (S.D. Fla. June 21, 2017) (citation omitted); Beach Imp. Corp. v. Hall, 143 Fla. 778, 782 (Fla. 1940).

A person cannot claim the quiet title if the property was adversely possessed by someone else at the time the tax deed was issued, and the suit started. [Deas v. Turner](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7563587103759222223), 56 So. 2d 337, 337 (Fla. 1952)

When trying to use laches as a defense a party needs to know that “The rule in Florida is well settled that passage of time alone is insufficient to constitute laches. There must be some injury or prejudice to the defendant as well.” [Niagara Fire Ins. Co. v. Allied Elec. Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5610686835825341355), 319 So. 2d 594, 595 (Fla. 3d DCA 1975); [Brown v. Semple](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=730338818208342432), 204 So. 2d 229, 233 (Fla. 3d DCA 1967)(emphasis added).

title: Replevin
description: [Fla. Stat. §78.055](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&Search_String=&URL=0000-0099/0078/Sections/0078.055.html); generally, [Fla. Stat. Ch. 78](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0000-0099/0078/0078ContentsIndex.html).
elements: A description of the claimed property that is sufficient to make possible its identification and a statement, to the best knowledge, information, and belief of the plaintiff of the value of such property and its location.

A statement that the plaintiff is the owner of the claimed property or is entitled to possession of it, describing the source of such title or right. If the plaintiff’s interest in such property is based on a written instrument, a copy of said instrument must be attached to the complaint.

A statement that the property is wrongfully detained by the defendant, the means by which the defendant came into possession thereof, and the cause of such detention according to the best knowledge, information, and belief of the plaintiff.
A statement that the claimed property has not been taken for a tax, assessment, or fine pursuant to law.
defenses: [Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: §95.11(3), Fla. Stat.

“Any person whose personal property is wrongfully detained by any other person or officer may have a writ of replevin to recover said personal property and any damages sustained by reason of the wrongful taking or detention as herein provided.” Fla. Stat. §78.01.
Replevin is a possessory action that requires in rem jurisdiction over the subject matter. Advantage Car Rental & Sales, Inc. v. Mitsubishi Motor Sales of Am., 664 So. 2d 46, 47 (Fla. 3d DCA 1995).

title: Rescission
description: The character or relationship of the parties; The making of the contract; The existence of fraud, mutual mistake, false representation, impossibility of performance, or other ground for rescission or cancellation; Plaintiff has rescinded the contract and notified defendant of such rescission; If the plaintiff has received benefits from the contract, the plaintiff should further allege an offer to restore those benefits to the defendant, if restoration is possible; and Plaintiff has no adequate remedy at law.
elements: The character or relationship of the parties;
The making of the contract;
The existence of fraud, mutual mistake, false representation, impossibility of performance, or other ground for rescission or cancellation;
Plaintiff has rescinded the contract and notified defendant of such rescission;
If the plaintiff has received benefits from the contract, the plaintiff should further allege an offer to restore those benefits to the defendant, if restoration is possible; and
Plaintiff has no adequate remedy at law.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(l), Fla. Stat. (four years). (3) Courts should not allow claims for rescission when plaintiff may pursue action at law for breach of warranty or contract. [Central Fla. Antenna Serv., Inc. v. A.M. Crabtree, 503 So.2d 1351, 1352 (Fla. 5th DCA 1987)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4224849453661639125). (4) Rescission is available only for fraud, accident or mistake. [Royal v. Parado, 462 So. 2d 849, 855 (Fla. 1st DCA 1985)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2271021289153726781); [AVVA-BC, LLC v. Amiel, 25 So.3d 7, 11 (Fla. 3d DCA 2009)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4263012180671879579); but see[Hibiscus Ass’n, Ltd., v. Bd. of Tr., 50 F.3d 908, 916 (11th Cir. 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=490065784158649252) (Florida law also allows rescission for breach of dependent covenant). (5) Rescission is generally not available when the parties cannot return to positions occupied prior to execution of contract [Paul Revere Life Ins. Co. v. Dietz, 785 F. Supp. 970, 972 (M.D. Fla. 1992)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8905358154687202748). But see [Bass v. Farish, 616 So.2d 1146, 1147 (Fla. 4th DCA 1993)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6805990481798592060) (noting an exception to the general rule when the inability of one party to restore to the status quo is caused by the fraud of the other party); [Bland v. Freightliner LLC, 206 F. Supp. 2d 1202, 1208-09 (M.D. Fla. 2002)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11199338065156462922) (stating that a court may grant rescission, despite the impossibility of restoration to the status quo, if the equities between the parties can be balanced).

title: Slander of Title
description: Slander of title is also called “title disparagement of property,” “slandered goods,” “trade libel,” and “injurious falsehood.” See[Collier Cty. Publ’g Co. v. Chapman, 318 So.2d 492, 494 (Fla. 2d DCA 1975)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17712856287358310024), cert. denied, 333 So. 2d 462 (1976).
elements: Defendant communicated to a third person;
A statement disparaging plaintiff’s title;
The statement is untrue; and
Defendant’s communication caused plaintiff to suffer actual damages.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(4)(g), Fla. Stat. (two years); see [Sailboat Key, Inc. v. Gardner, 378 So.2d 47 (Fla. 3d DCA 1979)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10924527830597993578)(slander of title and defamation claims share the same statute of limitations and defenses). (3) Truth is a complete defense to defamation claims. [Rosenberg v. American Bowling Congress, 589 F. Supp. 547, 551 (M.D. Fla. 1984)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17330855082235909969); [Trigeorgis v. Trigeorgis, 240 So.3d 772, 775 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=53242995180463715); Art. I, § 4, Fla. Const. (4) Statements made during a judicial proceeding are absolutely privileged provided that such statements are related to the proceeding’s subject matter. [Levin, Middlebrooks v. U.S. Fire Ins. Co., 639 So.2d 606, 607 (Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16849305990004782225) (absolute privilege extends to parties, witnesses, counsel, and judges); [Sun Life Assurance Co. of Can. v. Imperial Premium Fin., LLC, 904 F.3d 1197, 1218 (11th Cir. 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16888402844724281809); [Phillips v. Epic Aviation, LLC, 234 F. Supp. 3d 1174, 1208-15 (M.D. Fla. 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6916935218415441580).

Absolute privilege extends to statements made during labor grievance proceedings provided that such statements are related to the proceeding’s subject matter. [Hope v. Nat. Alliance Jacksonville 320, 649 So. 2d 897, 900 (Fla. 1st DCA 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=389824345445520955); [Walter v. Jet Aviation Flight Servs., Inc., No. 9:16-CV-81238-ROSENBERG/BRANNON, 2017 WL 3237375, at *9 n.5 (S.D. Fla. 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11649656300944573866). (6) Absolute privilege protects statements made by government officials in connection with their official duties. [Hauser v. Urchisin, 231 So. 2d 6, 8 (Fla. 1970)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14982816976873030078); [del Pino Allen v. Santelises, No. 3D18-1896, 2019 WL 942960, at *2 (Fla. 3d DCA Feb. 27, 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12172120590964341797). (7) Qualified privilege protects defamatory statements made by private individuals to the police or the state’s attorney prior to the institution of criminal charges. [Fridovich v. Fridovich, 598 So.2d 65, 69 (Fla. 1992)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2671126229261794235); [Lozada v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., 702 F. App’x. 904, 912 (11th Cir. 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2434718531090037006). (8) Qualified privilege protects defamatory statements that are published by a speaker in good faith, pursuant to a duty or special interest, and such privilege is not abused. [Thomas v. Tampa Bay Downs, Inc., 761 So.2d 401, 404 (Fla. 2d DCA 2000)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10116995592118442852); [Elbanna v. Captain D’s, LLC, No. 3:07–cv–926–J–32MCR, 2009 WL 435051, at *14 (M.D. Fla. Feb. 17, 2009)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3386837321807533564). (9) Statements of pure opinion based on known facts do not give rise to defamation claims. [Miami Child’s World, Inc. v. Sunbeam Television Corp., 669 So. 2d 336, 336 (Fla. 3d DCA 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8428423769510646820); [Turner v. Wells, 879 F.3d 1254, 1262 (11th Cir. 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9596876489821913613). (10) Minor inconsistencies in news reports are not actionable provided that report is substantially true and inaccuracies did not result from deliberate falsification or awareness of probable falsity. [Newton v. Florida Freedom Newspapers, Inc., 447 So.2d 906, 907 (Fla. 1st DCA 1984)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13897281155145818454). (11) § 770.01, Fla. Stat., requires five (5) days notice to a defendant prior to filing a libel suit.

title: Specific Performance
description: The Florida Supreme Court long ago held that specific performance is an equitable remedy that, under Florida law, is effectively the same as, and synonymous with, injunctive relief. Seaboard Oil Co. v. Donovon, 99 Fla. 1296, 1306 (Fla. 1930) (“an injunction against the breach of a contract is a negative decree of specific performance of the agreement, and the general rule is that the power and the duty of a court of equity to grant the former is measured by the same rules and practice as its power and duty to grant the latter relief.”); Thompson v. Shell Petroleum Corp., 130 Fla. 652 (Fla. 1938) (“An injunction restraining the breach of a contract is a negative specific enforcement of that contract. The jurisdiction of equity to grant such injunction is substantially coincident with its jurisdiction to compel a specific performance. Both are governed by the same doctrines and rules”). This proposition stands as strongly today. See [Northwestern Nat. Ins. Co. v. Greenspun, 330 So.2d 561, 563 (Fla. 3d DCA 1976)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2640700620983251114) (same);[Professional Golfer’s Ass’n of America v. Bankers Life & Cas. Co., 166 So.2d 488, 492 (Fla. 2d DCA 1964)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3656151973008573212) (explaining why “the same general rules apply to injunctions against the breach of a contract that apply to specific performance”) (citations omitted); [Grant v. U.S., 289 F. Supp. 2d 1361, 1367 (S.D. Fla. 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12555180391962138537) (“Specific performance is a form of injunctive relief”).
elements: Plaintiff and Defendant are parties to a contract;
Plaintiff performed its obligation under the contract or is ready, willing and able to perform;
Defendant refused to perform its obligation under the contract; and
No adequate remedy at law exists.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)and [Temporary Injunction Chapter](https://floridalitigationguide.com/injunction-temporary/). (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(5)(a), Fla. Stat. (one year). (3) “‘It is settled by an overwhelming weight of authority that, except in rare cases, where the right is clear and free from reasonable doubt, a mandatory injunction, commanding the defendant to do some positive act, will not be ordered except upon final hearing, and then only to execute the judgment or decree of the court.’” [Grant v. GHG014, LLC, 65 So. 3d 1066, 1067 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17870539637351348317)(emphasis added; citations omitted); Miami Bridge Co. v. Miami Beach Ry. Co., 12 So.2d 438, 443 (Fla. 1943). (4) Ambiguity: “Specific performance may be denied when a contract is unenforceable because, based on an ambiguity in the contract, the parties never reached a meeting of the minds regarding an essential term of the agreement.”[Boardwalk at Daytona Dev., LLC v. Paspalakis, 220 So.3d 457, 461 (Fla. 5th DCA 2016); King v. Bray, 867 So. 2d 1224, 1226 (Fla. 5th DCA 2004).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10222680819787463300)“The equitable remedy of specific performance is granted only where the parties have actually entered into an agreement that is definite and certain in all of its essential elements.” [People’s Tr. Ins. Co. v. Valentin, No. 3D19-58, 2020 WL 1542061, at *2 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2047664298613282533).

Noncompliance with Contract: Where plaintiff fails to comply with its contractual obligations, specific performance will be denied. [JNC Enters., Ltd. V. ICP 1, Inc., 777 So. 2d 1182, 1185 (Fla. 5th DCA 2001)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6226042167644238320), rev. denied, 792 So. 2d 1214 (Fla. 2001); [Muniz v. Crystal Lake Project, LLC, 947 So.2d 464, 470 (Fla. 3d DCA 2006)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6029088921719417837). (6) Unable to Comply: A court of equity will not demand that a contract be specifically enforced against a party who, due to future circumstances, is unable to comply with the agreement. [Camp. v. Parks, 314 So.2d 611, 615 (Fla. 4th DCA 1975)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2082099939760233075). (7) Doctrine of Unclean Hands: plaintiffs who seek a remedy in equity with “unclean hands,” which does not require the commission of a crime but only acts “condemned by honest and reasonable” persons, will be denied relief. [Roberts v. Roberts, 84 So.2d 717, 720 (Fla. 1956)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18417656984290964322); [McMichael v. Deutsche Bank Nat’l Tr. Co., 241 So.3d 179, 181 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1874503459094393105); [Nature’s Prods., Inc. v. Natrol, Inc., 990 F. Supp. 2d 1307, 1317 (S.D. Fla. 2013)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=69457891228544755). (8)Anticipatory Breach of Contract: A party that has repudiated its obligations under a contract cannot seek specific performance, as “anticipatory repudiation relieves the non-breaching party of its duty to further perform and creates in it an immediate cause of action for breach of contract.” [Twenty-Four Collection, Inc. v. M. Weinbaum Const., Inc., 427 So.2d 1110, 1111 (Fla. 3d DCA 1983)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2645983455282704960); accord[Banks. v. Lardin, 938 So.2d 571, 575 (Fla. 4th DCA 2006)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9967317492552547007)(“‘[W]here one party, even before the time for performance of the contract has arrived, renounces it to the other party, the latter may act on the renunciation, treat the contract as broken, and sue before the time for performance.’”) (citation omitted; emphasis added). (9) Injunctive relief is an extraordinary and drastic equitable remedy, which should be granted sparingly and only after the moving party has satisfied every one of the demanding prerequisites for such relief. [Florida High Sch. Activities Ass’n v. Kartenovich, 749 So.2d 1290, 1291 (Fla. 3d DCA 2000)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11583242321238579906). (10) A court may not enter a temporary injunction unless there are “[c]lear, definite and unequivocally sufficient factual findings support[ing] each of the four conclusions necessary to justify entry of a temporary injunction.” [Bellach v. Huggs of Naples, Inc., 704 So.2d 679, 680 (Fla. 2d DCA 1997)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4443357543935951983)(emphasis added); [Snibbe v. Napoleonic Society of Am., Inc., 682 So.2d 568, 570 (Fla. 2d DCA 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4088247618481838691)(“[t]he [court’s] findings must ‘do more than parrot each tine of the four-prong test’”). (11) “[P]laintiff must demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits as to asserted affirmative defenses as well as…elements of plaintiff’s prima facie case.” See, e.g., [Bradley v. Health Coalition, Inc., 687 So.2d 329, 333 (Fla. 3d DCA 1997)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13328075450369098651). Plaintiff bears the burden of establishing there is a clear legal right to the ultimate relief sought and a substantial likelihood of success on the merits. [Airport Executive Towers v. CIG Realty, Inc., 716 So.2d 311, 313 (Fla. 3d DCA 1998)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4212042372360274851); [Naegele Outdoor Advertising Co., Inc. v. City of Jacksonville, 659 So.2d 1046, 1047 (Fla. 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17386739960555071452)(advancing a merely colorable claim is not enough to show a substantial likelihood of success). (12) “Mandatory injunctions – [which require that a defendant do some positive act or that acts be undone] – are looked upon with disfavor, and the courts seem even more reluctant to issue them than prohibitory ones.” [Shaw v. Tampa Elec. Co., 949 So.2d 1066, 1070, n.3 (Fla. 2d DCA 2007)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8194209877665634102). (13) Plaintiff cannot enforce a money judgment or prevent defendant from dispersing assets pending litigation through a temporary injunction. [Proctor v. Eason, 651 So.2d 1301, 1301 (Fla. 2d DCA 1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17393479124017107818). (14) A tenant cannot seek specific performance of a lease against a landlord. [Cardinal Inv. Group, Inc. v. Giles, 813 So.2d 262, 263 (Fla. 4th DCA 2002)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4370495371678261303); [Craven v. TRG-Boynton Beach, Ltd., 925 So.2d 476, 481 (Fla. 4th DCA 2006)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10898030701371869550). (15) In addition to satisfaction of prima facie elements, Florida courts must also consider the following in determining whether to grant injunctive relief: (a) the nature of the interest to be protected, (b) the relative adequacy to the plaintiff of injunction and of other remedies, (c) any unreasonable delay by the plaintiff in bringing suit, (d) any related misconduct on the part of the plaintiff, (e) the relative hardship likely to result to defendant if an injunction is granted and to plaintiff if it is denied, (f) the interests of third persons and of the public, and (g) the practicability of framing and enforcing the order or judgment’’. [Davis v. Joyner, 409 So.2d 1193, 1195 (Fla. 4th DCA 1982)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3795585124361445338), citing Restatement (Second) of Torts § 936 (1979). (16) Unreasonable delay by a plaintiff in bringing suit may preclude the plaintiff from obtaining an injunction. Mercer v. Keynton, 127 So. 859 (Fla. 1930); [Mora v. Karr, 697 So.2d 887 (Fla. 4th DCA 1997)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2562892715730573019). (17) Courts must consider the harm the defendant will suffer by the issuance of an injunction balanced against the harm, if any, the plaintiff may suffer by a denial of an injunction. [Davis v. Joyner, 409 So.2d 1193, 1195 (Fla. 4th DCA 1982)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3795585124361445338).

title: Statutory Way of Necessity
description: [Blanton v. City of Pinellas Park](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1309014200567337458), 887 So. 2d 1224, 1228-29 (Fla. 2004).
defenses: [](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10540447568835379631)(1) [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)

Statute of Limitations: 704.04, Fla. Stat. (2023) (after either party file the claim, the circuit court determines if the easement exists). [Blanton v. City of Pinellas Park](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1309014200567337458), 887 So. 2d 1224, 1229-30 (Fla. 2004).

“To establish a statutory way of necessity, the owner of the landlocked parcel must show that the property is not served by a common law easement.” [Hancock v. Tipton](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2192795605011174743), 732 So. 2d 369, 373 (Fla. 2d DCA 1999) (emphasis added)(See [Bell v. Cox](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17228327058074092435), 642 So. 2d 1381, 1384 (Fla. 5th DCA 1994)).

The party seeking the statutory way of necessity has the burden of proof. [Goldman v. Lustig](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1432631800370164339), 237 So. 3d 381, 385 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018); [Palm Beach Polo Holdings, Inc. v. Equestrian Club Ests. Prop. Owners Ass’n, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4230131105083578530), 949 So. 2d 347, 349 (Fla. 4th DCA 2007).

Statutory way of necessity cannot be granted in the absence of absolute necessity. [Messer v. Sander](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13665732086726907391), 144 So. 3d 566, 569 (Fla. 1st DCA 2014); [Palm Beach Polo Holdings, Inc. v. Equestrian Club Ests. Prop. Owners Ass’n, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4230131105083578530), 949 So. 2d 347, 349-50 (Fla. 4th DCA 2007).

“[T]he statutory way of necessity exists only when the lands are being used or desired to be used for the purposes specified in the statute.” [Staten v. Gonzalez-Falla](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11200585137205049559), 904 So. 2d 498, 501 (Fla. 1st DCA 2005)(citing [Hunt v. Smith](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17052391902819869307), 137 So. 2d 232, 233-34 (Fla. 2d DCA 1962))(emphasis added).

When claiming statutory way of necessity, a party cannot use sovereign immunity as a defense. [Fla. Water Mgmt. Dist. v. Layton](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16197625662218820441), 402 So. 2d 597, 598-99 (Fla. 2d DCA 1981).

“A statutory way of necessity does not require a common source of title and is dependant upon the existence of numerous factors that are not necessary to the creation of a common law way of necessity.” [Cirelli v. Ent](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9759399922909685421), 885 So. 2d 423, 428 (Fla. 5th DCA 2004)(emphasis added).

[T]he legislature intended to include the state and its agencies within the meaning of “persons.” Maradiaga v. Brevard Cnty. Sch. Bd., 2007 WL 9719456, *3 (M.D. Fla. Aug. 24, 2007); [Florida Water Mgmt. Dist. v. Layton](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16197625662218820441), 402 So. 2d 597 (Fla. 2d DCA 1981)(emphasis added).

“The rights of the owners of an easement over a “servient estate” are not absolute and unlimited. They are limited so that each party may reasonably enjoy his respective property rights.” [Tortoise Island Communities, Inc. v. Roberts](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4963705945110993946), 394 So. 2d 568, 569 (Fla. 5th DCA 1981) (citing [Costin v. Branch](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2130449663321267193), 373 So. 2d 370, 371 (Fla. 1st DCA 1979))(emphasis added).

A Statutory way of necessity cannot be extinguished by Marketable Record Title Act(MRTA.) [Blanton v. City of Pinellas Park](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1309014200567337458), 887 So. 2d 1224, 1233 (Fla. 2004); [Cirelli v. Ent](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9759399922909685421), 885 So. 2d 423, 426 (Fla. 5th DCA 2004).

title: Strict Liability
description: Manufacturer or seller places a defective product on the market; The defective product is sold in an unreasonably dangerous condition; The product reaches the plaintiff without substantial change in the condition in which the product is sold; and The defect is the proximate cause of the plaintiff’s injury.
elements: Manufacturer or seller places a defective product on the market;
The defective product is sold in an unreasonably dangerous condition;
The product reaches the plaintiff without substantial change in the condition in which the product is sold; and
The defect is the proximate cause of the plaintiff’s injury.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(e), Fla. Stat. (four years). (3) The statute of repose bars product liability actions based on harm “allegedly caused by a product with an expected useful life of 10 years or less, if the harm was caused by exposure to or use of the product more than 12 years after delivery of the product to its first purchaser or lessee who was not engaged in the business of selling or leasing the product or of using the product as a component in the manufacture of another product,’’ unless the product is specifically exempted as having a useful life greater than 10 years. § 95.031(2)(b), Fla. Stat; [Dominguez v. Hayward Indus., Inc., 201 So.3d 100, 101 (Fla. 3d DCA 2015)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15641467915995518012); [Competitor Liaison Bureau, Inc. v. Cessna Aircraft Co., No. 6:08–cv–2165–Orl–28GJK, 2011 WL 1344455, at *2 (M.D. Fla. Apr. 11, 2011)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18331060024543264921). (4) Product misuse will diminish the plaintiff’s recovery through comparative negligence. [Standard Havens Products, Inc. v. Benitez, 648 So.2d 1192, 1197 (Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13026275804224884093); [Cerrato v. Nutribullet, LLC, No. 8:16–cv–3077–T–24 JSS, 2017 WL 5164898, at *3 (M.D. Fla. Nov. 7, 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1236747060291594315). (5) Assumption of the risk will diminish the plaintiff’s recovery through comparative negligence. [Blackburn v. Dorta, 348 So.2d 287, 293 (Fla. 1977)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3342236169393332157); [Petruzzella v. Church on the Rock of Palm Coast, Inc., 219 So.3d 239, 241 (Fla. 5th DCA 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2942735339362210538). (6) Manufacturers are not liable for damages caused by products that cannot be made safe for its ordinary and intended uses when the product is still useful despite the product’s known risks. Restatement (Second) of Torts, § 402A Comment K (1986); [Zanzuri v. G.D. Searle & Co., 748 F. Supp. 1511, 1518 (S.D. Fla. 1990)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11183137297918705132) (listing federal requirements of Comment K defense); [Adams v. G. D. Searle & Co., Inc., 576 So.2d 728, 733-734 (Fla. 2d DCA 1991)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2438100924840668188) (listing Florida requirement for Comment K defense). (7) The economic loss doctrine is limited to products liability cases and bars causes of action in tort unless the defective product injures a person or damages property other than the defective product itself. [Tiara Condominium Assoc., Inc. v. March & McClennan Cos. Inc., 110 So.3d 399 (Fla. 2013)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2579241066312764846); [King v. Bencie, 752 F. App’x. 881, 883 (11th Cir. 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15173761193569177629). (8) Consent is a defense to strict liability claims. Restatement (Second) of Torts § 892 (1965).

title: Strict Liability – Design Defect
description: Manufacturer or seller places a defective product on the market; The defective product is sold in an unreasonably dangerous condition; The product reaches the plaintiff without substantial change in the condition in which the product is sold; and The defect is the proximate cause of the plaintiff’s injury.
elements: Manufacturer or seller places a defective product on the market;
The defective product is sold in an unreasonably dangerous condition;
The product reaches the plaintiff without substantial change in the condition in which the product is sold; and
The defect is the proximate cause of the plaintiff’s injury.
defenses: [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3), Fla. Stat. (four years).
Statute of Repose: § 95.031(2)(b), Fla. Stat. (twelve years).

A seller can successfully plead an affirmative defense to a strict liability design defect claim for a product incapable of being made safe if they establish that: (1) the product’s “benefits outweigh its known risks” as of the distribution date; (2) It is “incapable of being made safe,”; (3) It is “properly prepared and marketed,”; and (4) It is “accompanied by a proper warning.” [LaBarre v. Bristol-Myers Squibb Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6095713834426617316), 544 F. App’x 120, 126 (3d Cir. 2013); see also [Adams v. G.D. Searle & Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2438100924840668188), 576 So. 2d 728, 733 (Fla. 2d DCA. 1991); Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A, cmt. k. (1965).

Under the Second Restatement’s consumer-expectation theory, a product is defectively designed if “the product did not perform as safely as an ordinary consumer would expect when used in the intended or reasonably foreseeable manner.” [Grieco v. Daiho Sangyo, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11857772913693287784), 344 So. 3d 11, 19 (Fla. 4th DCA 2022) (quoting [Aubin v. Union Carbide Corp., 177 So. 3d 489](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7699595127436170266), 504 (Fla. 2015)).

The Third Restatement’s “risk/utility” test requires the factfinder to determine whether a “reasonable alternative design” was available to the manufacturer. This was rejected by the Florida Supreme Court in favor of the Second Restatement’s Consumer expectation test. [Aubin v. Union Carbide Corp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7699595127436170266), 177 So. 3d 489, 512 (Fla. 2015).

title: Strict Liability – Failure to Warn
description: To prevail on a failure to warn claim, a plaintiff must prove: (1) that the warnings were inadequate; (2) that the inadequacy of the warnings proximately caused the injury; and (3) that the plaintiff suffered an injury by using the product. [Colville v. Pharmacia & Upjohn Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11798578096040205286), 565 F. Supp. 2d 1314, 1320 (N.D. Fla. 2008); see also [Wright v. Howmedica Osteonics Corp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5918354238062467679), 741 F. App’x 624, 626 (11th Cir. 2018).
elements: Manufacturer or seller places a defective product on the market;
The defective product is sold in an unreasonably dangerous condition;
The product reaches the plaintiff without substantial change in the condition in which the product is sold; and
The defect is the proximate cause of the plaintiff’s injury.
defenses: [Fla.R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3), Fla. Stat. (four years).
Statute of Repose: § 95.031(2)(b), Fla. Stat. (twelve years).

A distributor of an inherently dangerous commodity must provide fair and adequate warning of its dangerous potentialities to its users, and is strictly liable for injuries caused by the failure to do so. [Tampa Drug Co v. Wait](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17683037034742862751), 103 So. 2d 603, 607 (Fla. 1958); see also [Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Hughes Supply, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15312084666229146232), 358 So. 2d 1339 (Fla. 1978).

Manufacturers are strictly liable for failing to warn of dangerous contents in their products “which could damage or injure even when the product is not used for its intended purpose.” [High v. Westinghouse Elec. Corp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17891862445002788662), 610 So. 2d 1259, 1262 (Fla. 1992).

An adequate warning should contain wording directed to the “significant dangers arising from failure to use the product in the prescribed manner, such as the risk of serious injury or death.” [Grieco v. Daiho Sangyo, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11857772913693287784), 344 So. 3d 11, 20 (Fla. 4th DCA 2022).

There is no duty to warn of obvious or known dangers. [Scheman-Gonzalez v. Saber Mfg. Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13238930404444945626), 816 So. 2d 1133, 1139 (Fla. 4th DCA 2002).

“[I]n pleading the elements of a failure-to-warn claim in the context of a medical device, a plaintiff must allege that the manufacturer failed to warn the patient’s physician of the risks associated with a medical product’s prescribed use, not its alleged defects… Further, because Florida has adopted the learned intermediary doctrine, the manufacturer’s duty to warn runs to the physician, not to the patient…” [Zamora v. AAP Implants, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=312079991279654071), No. 24-CV-21625, 2024 WL 4851352, at *3 (S.D. Fla. Nov. 21, 2024), report and recommendation adopted, No. 24-CV-21625, 2024 WL 5040719 (S.D. Fla. Dec. 9, 2024); see also [Beale v. Biomet, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16035791582599722998), 492 F. Supp. 2d 1360, 1368 (S.D. Fla. 2007).

title: Strict Liability – Manufacturing Defect
description: A product is unreasonably dangerous because of a manufacturing defect if it does not conform to its intended design and fails to perform as safely as the intended design would have performed. Reyes v. Barnett Outdoors, LLC, No. 8:20-cv-763-SDM-TGW, 2022 WL 1619430, at *8 (M.D. Fla. Mar. 29, 2022).
elements: Manufacturer or seller places a defective product on the market;
The defective product is sold in an unreasonably dangerous condition;
The product reaches the plaintiff without substantial change in the condition in which the product is sold; and
The defect is the proximate cause of the plaintiff’s injury.
defenses: [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3), Fla. Stat. (four years).
Statute of Repose: § 95.031(2)(b), Fla. Stat. (twelve years).

A claimant may not commence an action for injury caused by a product with an expected useful life of 10 years or less, if the harm was caused by exposure to the product more than 12 years after its delivery to its first purchaser or lessee who was not engaged in the business of selling or leasing the product or of using the product as a component in the manufacture of another product. § 95.031, Fla. Stat.

Assumption of Risk where the user voluntarily and unreasonably proceeds to encounter a known danger is a defense. [West v. Caterpillar Tractor Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13011785084594536711), 336 So. 2d 80, 90 (Fla. 1976).

Contributory/ Comparative negligence of the user or consumer or bystander in the sense of a “failure to discover a defect, or to guard against the possibility of its existence, is not a defense.” [West v. Caterpillar Tractor Co.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13011785084594536711), 336 So. 2d 80, 90 (Fla. 1976).

If the plaintiff misused the product in a way that was not reasonably foreseeable by the manufacturer, and this misuse is a substantial proximate cause of the plaintiff’s injuries or damages, this can serve as a valid defense. [Gonzalez v. G.A. Braun, Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4993028013264294905), 608 So. 2d 125, 126 (Fla. 3d DCA 1992).

“The manufacturer’s liability also extends to bystanders who are injured by the defective product.” [Disarro v. EzriCare, LLC,](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16519803106419993169)2:23-CV-230-JES-KCD, 2023 WL 4737010, at *6 (M.D. Fla. July 25, 2023).

title: Subrogation, Equitable
description: Florida law also recognizes claims for conventional subrogation, which arise where a contract conveys to the party paying the debt of another the rights and remedies of the original creditor. See, e.g., [Dade County School Board v. Radio Station WQBA, 731 So. 2d 638, 646 (Fla. 1999)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11323804062576171249).
elements: Plaintiff is subrogated to the rights of the injured party (the “subrogee”);
The subrogee made the payment to protect his or her own interest,
The subrogee did not act as a volunteer,
The subrogee was not primarily liable for the debt,
The subrogee paid off the entire debt,
Subrogation would not work any injustice to the rights of a third party, and
As a result, the subrogee (party discharging the debt) stands in the shoes of the person whose claims have been discharged and thus succeeds to the right and priorities of the original creditor.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(p), Fla. Stat. (four years). (3) “[A] settlement executed by the insured cannot act as a bar to an action for subrogation by the insurer against a third-party tortfeasor if, prior to the settlement, the tortfeasor learns of the insurer’s perfected subrogation rights.” See, e.g., [Lincoln Nat. Health and Cas. v. Mitsubishi, 778 So. 2d 392, 395 (Fla. 5th DCA 2001)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10538321355196708554).

“Subrogation in equity is not available to a mere volunteer or stranger who, without any duty or obligation to intervene and without being so requested, pays the debt of another.” [Dade County Sch. Bd. v. Radio Station WQBA, 731 So. 2d 638, 646 (Fla. 1999)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11323804062576171249); [Tank Tech, Inc.v. Valley Testing, L.L.C., 244 So.3d 383, 389 (Fla. 2d DCA 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11950801477080904831).

If the plaintiff/subrogor has no rights against the third party, the subrogee has no rights against such party. [Dade County Sch. Bd. v. Radio Station WQBA, 731 So. 2d 638, 647 (Fla. 1999)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11323804062576171249); [Welch v. Complete Care Corp., 818 So.2d 645, 648 (Fla. 2nd DCA 2002)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3429437924561028176) (6) Plaintiff does not allege that it is subrogated to the rights of the injured party. [Florida Farm Bureau General Ins. Co. v. Ins. Co. of North America, 763 So. 2d 429, 436 (Fla. 5th DCA 2000)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17855731239844712994).

title: Temporary Injunction
description: Specific performance is an equitable remedy that, under Florida law, is effectively the same as, and synonymous with, injunctive relief. Seaboard Oil Co. v. Donovan, 99 Fla. 1296, 1306 (Fla. 1930)(“an injunction against the breach of a contract is a negative decree of specific performance of the agreement, and the general rule is that the power and the duty of a court of equity to grant the former is measured by the same rules and practice as its power and duty to grant the latter relief.”); Thompson v. Shell Petroleum Corp., 130 Fla. 652 (1938)(“An injunction restraining the breach of a contract is a negative specific enforcement of that contract. The jurisdiction of equity to grant such injunction is substantially coincident with its jurisdiction to compel a specific performance. Both are governed by the same doctrines and rules”). This proposition stands as strongly today. See, e.g., [Northwestern Nat. Ins. Co. v. Greenspun](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2640700620983251114), 330 So. 2d 561, 563 (Fla. 3d DCA 1976) (same); [Professional Golfer’s Ass’n of America v. Bankers Life & Cas. Co., 166 So. 2d 488, 492 (Fla. 2d DCA 1964)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3656151973008573212)(explaining why “the same general rules apply to injunctions against the breach of a contract that apply to specific performance”)(citations omitted); [Grant v. U.S., 289 F. Supp. 2d 1361, 1367 (S.D. Fla. 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12555180391962138537)(“Specific performance is a form of injunctive relief”).
elements: Plaintiff will suffer irreparable harm;
Plaintiff has no adequate remedy at law;
Plaintiff has a substantial likelihood of success on the merits; and
A temporary injunction will serve the public interest.
defenses: Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.

Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(p), Fla. Stat. (four years); [Park v. City of W. Melbourne](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10228465002153364150), 999 So. 2d 673, 677 (Fla. 5th DCA 2008); [Hollywood Lakes Section Civic Ass’n, Inc. v. City of Hollywood, 676 So. 2d 500, 501 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5816033888961628090).

Injunctive relief is an extraordinary and drastic equitable remedy, which should be granted sparingly and only after the moving party has satisfied every one of the demanding prerequisites for such relief. [Salazar v. Hometeam Pest Def., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16362343008876639957), 230 So. 3d 619, 621 (Fla. 2d DCA 2017); [Florida High Sch. Activities Assoc. v. Kartenovich, 749 So.2d 1290, 1291 (Fla. 3d DCA 2000); Nivel Parts & Mnf. Co., LLC, v. Textron, No. 3:17–cv–146–J–32JRK, 2017 WL 1552034, *1 (M.D. Fla. May 1, 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11583242321238579906); [Hochstein v. City of Miami Beach](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15067683307917472001), 758 F. Supp. 3d 1348, 1354 (S.D. Fla. 2024).

A court may not enter a temporary injunction unless there are “[c]lear, definite and unequivocally sufficient factual findings support[ing] each of the four conclusions necessary to justify entry of a temporary injunction.”[Bellach v. Huggs of Naples, Inc., 704 So.2d 679, 680 (Fla. 2d DCA 1997)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4443357543935951983)(emphasis added); [Leposky v. Ego](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17038433124731971348), 348 So. 3d 1160, 1162 (Fla. 4th DCA 2022); [St. Brendan High Sch., Inc. v. Neff](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16028999476710198159), 275 So. 3d 220, 222 (Fla. 3d DCA 2019); see also[Snibbe v. Napoleonic Society of Am., Inc](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4088247618481838691)., 682 So.2d 568, 570 (Fla. 2d DCA 1996)(“[t]he [court’s] findings must ‘do more than parrot each tine of the four-prong test’”); see also [Tesoro Property Owner’s Ass’n v. Tesoro Commons, LLC, 237 So.3d 403, 404 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9334712966110626074).

“[P]laintiff must demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits as to asserted affirmative defenses as well as…elements of plaintiff’s prima facie case.” See, e.g., [Bradley v. Health Coalition, Inc](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13328075450369098651)., 687 So.2d 329, 333 (Fla. 3d DCA 1997)(emphasis added); [Salazar v. Hometeam Pest Def., Inc.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16362343008876639957), 230 So. 3d 619, 622 (Fla. 2d DCA 2017). Plaintiff bears the burden of establishing there is a clear legal right to the ultimate relief sought and a substantial likelihood of success on the merits. [Airport Executive Towers v. CIG Realty, Inc., 716 So.2d 311, 313 (Fla. 3d DCA 1998)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4212042372360274851); see also [Naegele Outdoor Advertising Co., Inc. v. City of Jacksonville](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17386739960555071452), 659 So.2d 1046, 1047 (Fla. 1995) (advancing a merely colorable claim is not enough to show a substantial likelihood of success);[Silver Rose Entertainment, Inc. v. Clay County, 646 So.2d 246, 248 (Fla. 1st DCA 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=296489598593150158)(same).

“Mandatory injunctions – [which require that a defendant do some positive act or that acts be undone] – are looked upon with disfavor, and the courts seem even more reluctant to issue them than prohibitory ones.” [Shaw v. Tampa Elec. Co., 949 So.2d 1066, 1070, n.3 (Fla. 2d DCA 2007)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8194209877665634102)(emphasis added); [Bull Motors, L.L.C. v. Brown](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14061570015907482520), 152 So. 3d 32, 35 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014); [Grant v. GHG014, LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17870539637351348317), 65 So. 3d 1066, 1067 (Fla. 4th DCA 2010); see also [FHR TB, LLC v. TB Isle Resort, LP., 865 F.Supp.2d 1172, 1192(S.D. Fla 2011)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2979377835100483656)(moving party will face a particularly heavy burden of persuasion).

Injunctive relief is not available “where the injury to the movant is seeking to prevent is purely monetary” or “when the right to the injunction is premised on a speculative, future event.” [Lutsky v. Schoenwetter, 172 So.3d 534 (Fla. 3d DCA 2015)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14487694346404606284)(emphasis added)(citations omitted); [Fla. Ass’n of Realtors v. Orange Cnty.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2933559365477279198), 350 So. 3d 115, 130 (Fla. 5th DCA 2022).

Plaintiff cannot enforce a money judgment or prevent defendant from dispersing assets pending litigation trough a temporary injunction. See [Proctor v. Eason](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17393479124017107818), 651 So. 2d 1301, 1301 (Fla. 2d DCA 1995); [Briceno v. Bryden Invs., Ltd.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4375350068731709659), 973 So. 2d 614, 616 (Fla. 3d DCA 2008).

A tenant cannot seek specific performance of a lease against a landlord. E.g., [Cardinal Inv. Group, Inc. v. Giles](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4370495371678261303), 813 So.2d 262, 263 (Fla. 4th DCA 2002); [Craven v. TRG-Boynton Beach, Ltd.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10898030701371869550), 925 So. 2d 476, 481 (Fla. 4th DCA 2006).

In addition to satisfaction of prima facie elements, Florida courts must also consider the following in determining whether to grant injunctive relief: “(a) the nature of the interest to be protected, (b) the relative adequacy to the plaintiff of injunction and of other remedies, (c) any unreasonable delay by the plaintiff in bringing suit, (d) any related misconduct on the part of the plaintiff, (e) the relative hardship likely to result to defendant if an injunction is granted and to plaintiff if it is denied, (f) the interests of third persons and of the public, and (g) the practicability of framing and enforcing the order or judgment’’. [Davis v. Joyner, 409 So. 2d 1193, 1195 (Fla. 4th DCA 1982)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3795585124361445338), citing Restatement (Second) of Torts § 936 (1979).

Unreasonable delay by a plaintiff in bringing suit may preclude the plaintiff from obtaining an injunction. [Mora v. Karr, 697 So.2d 887 (Fla. 4th DCA 1997)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2562892715730573019).

Courts must consider the harm the defendant will suffer by the issuance of an injunction balanced against the harm, if any, the plaintiff may suffer by a denial of an injunction. [Davis v. Joyner, 409 So.2d 1193, 1195 (Fla. 4th DCA 1982)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3795585124361445338).

A plaintiff with unclean hands may not obtain an injunction. Also, Plaintiff does not come into this suit with clean hands. [Williamson v. Williamson, 367 So.2d 1016, 1018 (Fla. 1979)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=1882975925745199768)( “[H]e who seeks equity must stand before the court with ‘clean hands’ and ‘he who seeks equity must do equity.’”);[PNC Bank, Nat’l Ass’n v. Smith, 225 So.3d 294, 295 (Fla. 5th DCA 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13619099079954567311).

“No temporary injunction shall be entered unless a bond is given by the movant in an amount the court deems proper, conditioned for the payment of costs and damages sustained by the adverse party if the adverse party is wrongfully enjoined.” Fla.R.Civ.P. 1.610(b) (emphasis added). However, temporary injunctive relief may be granted without the posting of a bond in the following situations: 1) injunctions entered “on the pleading of a municipality or the state or any officer, agency, or political subdivision thereof”; or 2) injunctions “issued solely to prevent physical injury or abuse of a natural person.” Id.; [Shir Law Grp., P.A. v. Carnevale](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6225642405567676768), 317 So. 3d 211, 213 (Fla. 3d DCA 2021); [Vital Pharm., Inc. v. Prof’l Supplements, LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13240667469612520646), 210 So. 3d 766, 767 (Fla. 4th DCA 2017); see also [Williams v. Victim Justice, P.C., 198 So.3d 822, 826 (Fla. 2d DCA 2016)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=164348483816343984).

The trial court cannot waive the bond requirement nor can it comply by setting a nominal amount. E.g., [Florida High School Activities Ass’n v. Mander](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2662602443691365692), 932 So.2d 314, 316 (Fla. 2d DCA 2006) (citing cases); see also [Forrest v. Citi Residential Lending, Inc., 73 So.3d 269, 279 (Fla. 2d DCA 2011); Castillo Grand Residences Condo. Ass’n, Inc. v. Stern, 304 So. 3d 23, 28 (Fla. 4th DCA 2020); Pendergraft v. C.H., 225 So. 3d 420, 421 (Fla. 5th DCA 2017).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6414268432200793744)

A party may move to dissolve or modify a temporary injunction at any time and such a motion must be heard within five days of application. Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.610(d). [Planned Parenthood of Greater Orlando, Inc. v. MMB Props.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11606344109264957645), 211 So. 3d 918, 924 (Fla. 2017).

Injunctive relief is a remedy and not an independent stand alone cause of action. See, e.g., [Pronman v. Styles, No. 12–80674–CIV, 2015 WL 58629, *11 (S.D. Fla. 2015)(Marra, K.)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5822172964622562350).

“A temporary injunction will not be overturned absent a clear abuse of discretion.” [Ames v. Ames, 204 So.3d 132, 133 (Fla. 4th DCA 2016); Videla v. Ogino](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17791659747148609954), 2023 WL 4339710, *1 (Fla. 3d DCA July 5, 2023); [Garcia v. Soto](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4517903696743747563), 337 So. 3d 355, 359 (Fla. 4th DCA 2022).

title: Tortious Interference: 1. With Advantageous Business Relationship
description: Plaintiff has a business relationship, not necessarily evidenced by an enforceable contract; Defendant has knowledge of the relationship; Defendant intentionally and unjustifiably interfered with the relationship; and Plaintiff suffered damages.
elements: Plaintiff has a business relationship, not necessarily evidenced by an enforceable contract;
Defendant has knowledge of the relationship;
Defendant intentionally and unjustifiably interfered with the relationship; and
Plaintiff suffered damages.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(p), Fla. Stat. (four years). (3) Acts occurring during a judicial proceeding are absolutely privileged and cannot give rise to tortious interference claims. [Davis v. Bailynson, 268 So. 3d 762, 769 (Fla. 4th DCA 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17820739546361971531); [Levin, Middlebrooks v. U.S. Fire Ins. Co., 639 So. 2d 606, 608 (Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16849305990004782225); but see [DelMonico v. Traynor, 116 So.3d 1205, 1220 (Fla. 2013)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15695827028712735345) (holding that statements made during ex-parte, out-of-court questioning of potential witnesses are subject only to qualified privilege). (4) Plaintiff cannot bring tortious interference claim when a contract provision expressly reserves the right of interference. [McCurdy v. Collis, 508 So. 2d 380, 383 (Fla. 1st DCA 1987)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4188858777600808814), rev. denied, 518 So. 2d 1274 (Fla. 1987); [11611 Bonita Beach Rd. SE Assocs., LLC v. Pine Island Crossing, LLC, No. 2:14–cv–625–FtM–38DNF, 2015 WL 757844, at *3 (M.D. Fla. Feb. 23, 2015)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17048234968702307239). (5) An agent that gives, on request by his or her principal, “honest advice” in his or her principal’s best interest to breach an existing relationship is not liable for tortious interference. [Scussel v. Balter, 386 So.2d 1227, 1228 (Fla. 3d DCA 1980)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17083890466225280019); [Westgate Resorts, Ltd. v. Reed Hein & Assocs., LLC, No: 6:18-cv-1088-Orl-31DCI, 2018 WL 5279156, at *4 (M.D. Fla. Oct. 24, 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11847647331723521912); Restatement (Second) of Torts § 772 (1965). (6) Plaintiff cannot bring a tortious interference claim against a defendant that is a party to the business relationship at issue. [Ethyl Corp. v. Balter, 386 So. 2d 1220, 1224 (Fla. 3d DCA 1980)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5749291592517869420), cert. denied, 425 U.S. 955 (1981); [Seminole Masonry, LLC v. Hodges, No. 18-60368-Civ-Scola, 2019 WL 687918, at *5 (S.D. Fla. Feb. 19, 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16432494974858844950).

Privileged or justified conduct does not give rise to tortious interference claim. [VVIG, Inc. v. Alvarez, No. 18-23109-CIV, 2019 WL 5063441, at *7 (S.D. Fla. Oct. 9, 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6047512676102267261); [Heavener, Ogier Servs., Inc. v. R.W. Florida Regions, Inc., 418 So. 2d 1074, 1077 (Fla. 5th DCA 1982)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6889343063040529876); see also Restatement (Second) of Torts § 768 (1965).

Defendant acting to protect his or her own economic or financial interests is not liable for tortious interference. [Bruce v. American Dev. Corp., 408 So. 2d 857, 858 (Fla. 3d DCA 1982)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9713437481964636456); [Collier HMA Physician Mgmt., LLC v. NCH Healthcare Sys., Inc., No: 2:18-cv-408-FtM-38MRM, 2019 WL 277733, at *9 (M.D. Fla. Jan. 22, 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15829176576768834482); Restatement (Second) of Torts § 769 (1965). (9) Plaintiff cannot premise claim on alleged interference with a contract that is terminable at will provided that interference is lawful competition. [Adler Consulting Corp. v. Executive Life Ins. Co., 483 So. 2d 501, 502 (Fla. 3d DCA 1986)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14553862746130990012).

Defendant’s settlement of a lawsuit that adversely affects plaintiff’s business interests does not give rise to tortious interference claim. [Paparone v. Bankers Life & Casualty, Co., 496 So. 2d 865, 868 (Fla. 2d DCA 1986)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9228352851597698565). (11) Plaintiffs cannot establish a tortious interference claim by alleging that defendant interfered with an amorphous class of customers, but rather must establish the existence of a business relationship with “identifiable customers”. [Ferguson Trans. v. North American Van Lines, 687 So. 2d 821, 821-822 (Fla. 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13331446970382267481); [Ethan Allen v. Georgetown Manor, 647 So. 2d 812, 815 (Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=717571510578138266) ( “In Florida, a plaintiff may properly bring a cause of action alleging tortious interference with present or prospective customers but no cause of action exists for tortious interference with a business’s relationship to the community at large. As a general rule, an action for tortious interference with a business relationship requires a business relationship evidenced by an actual and identifiable understanding or agreement which in all probability would have been completed if the defendant had not interfered.”)(internal citation omitted)(emphasis added); [B & D Nutritional Ingredients, Inc. v. Unique Bio Ingredients, LLC, 758 Fed.Appx. 785, 791 (11th Cir. 2018)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15685953264971909408).

Even if the defendant is aware of the existing business relationship, the defendant will not be liable for tortious interference with that relationship unless there is evidence that the defendant intended to procure a breach of the contract. [University of W. Fla. Bd. of Tr. v. Habegger, 125 So.3d 323, 326 (Fla. 1st DCA 2013)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13822216763290232575); [Chicago Title Ins. Co. v. Alday–Donalson Title Co. of Fla., Inc., 832 So.2d 810, 814 (Fla. 2d DCA 2002).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=7122688955784170885)

title: Trusts, Constructive Trust
description: There is no statute of limitations for the imposition of a constructive trust. Instead, the doctrine of laches applies. See [Small Bus. Admin. v. Echevarria, 864 F. Supp. 1254, 1265 (S.D. Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11969192788215270793)(citing Ruff v. Lake Abstract Guar. Co., 101 B.R. 763 (Bankr. M.D. Fla. 1989)); but see[Grable v. Nunez, 64 So. 2d 154, 159 (Fla. 1953)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3842108032784501544)(‘Constructive trusts are subject to statutes of limitation, and the period of limitation commences to run from the time when the trust came into being.’)(citations omitted); [Collinson v. Miller, 903 So. 2d 221, 229 (Fla. 2d DCA 2005)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13007751588093982303)(claim for constructive trust based on a breach of contract is four years from the time the cause of action accrues). Constructive or resulting trusts involving real estate can be based on parol evidence. See[Stonely v. Moore, 851 So. 2d 905, 906 (Fla. 3d DCA 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4599070192872117386). Heirs to a decedent’s assets don’t need to prove a constructive trust in order maintain lis pendens. See [Von-Mitschke-Collande v. Kramer, 869 So. 2d 1246, 1251 (Fla. 3d DCA 2004](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6025690102876657483)). Before one can successfully impress a constructive trust, there must be an identifiable res on which the trust can be impressed. [In re: Financial Federated Title and Trust, Inc., 347 F.3d 880, 891 (11th Cir. 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=889958887113309317).
elements: Plaintiff and defendant share a confidential relationship through which;
Defendant makes a promise, express or implied;
To transfer property to the plaintiff and causing reliance thereon; and
Defendant is unjustly enriched by failing to deliver the property.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/) (2) The doctrine of laches, and not the statute of limitations, applies to claims for constructive trust. Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d)(discussed in § 56); [Small Bus. Admin. v. Echevarria, 864 F. Supp. 1254, 1265 (S.D. Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11969192788215270793); [Mootilal Rahmit & Sons Contracting, Ltd. v. Mohammed, No. 13–23432–CIV, 2014 WL 3439742, at*10 n.3 (S.D. Fla. 2014)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13474421913575598419). (3) A constructive trust may only be imposed on specific or identifiable property or property which can be clearly traced in assets of the defendant. [G.W. Palmer & Co. v. Fla. Fresh Produce Corp., No. 217CV657FTM29MRM, 2019 WL 480501, at *5 (M.D. Fla. Feb. 7, 2019)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=5116225314867783645); [Bank of Am. v. Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11969192788215270793). (4) A constructive trust may be imposed only on clearly traced assets. See [Small Bus. Admin. v. Echevarria, 864 F. Supp. 1254, 1265 (S.D. Fla. 1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11969192788215270793); [U.S. v. Okonkwo, 2016 WL 6984273, at *3 (M.D. Fla. Plaintiff has an adequate remedy at law. [Bender v. CenTrust Mortg. See [Steinhardt v. Steinhardt, 445 So. 2d 352, 357 (Fla. 3d DCA 1984)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10536529334060701073), rev. denied, 456 So. 2d 1181 (Fla. 1984); Constructive or resulting trusts involving real estate can be based on parol evidence. elements: The parties actually intend to create a trust relationship;

title: Unfair Competition
description: The following claims share identical elements: (a) common law trade name, service mark and trade mark infringement; (b) common law unfair competition; and (c) Lanham Act trade name, service mark and trade mark infringement. See[American United Life Ins. Co. v. American United Ins. Co., 731 F. Supp. 480, 486 (S.D. Fla. 1990)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3288857712755399751); [Ocean Bio-Chem, Inc. v. Turner Network Television, Inc., 741 F. Supp. 1546, 1553 (S.D. Fla. 1990)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14562256072917238077). A “trade name” describes an entity or person, and applies to a business and its good will. A “service mark” describes the services provided by an entity or person and a “trade mark” reflects marketable goods. See [Blanding Auto. Ctr., Inc. v. Blanding Auto., Inc., 568 So.2d 490, 492 n.1 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2617998564948568465).
elements: Plaintiff is the prior user of the trade name, service mark or trade mark (collectively, “trade symbol”);
Plaintiff’s trade symbol is arbitrary or suggestive or has acquired secondary meaning;

Defendant is using a confusingly similar trade symbol to identify a similar good marketed or services rendered in competition with the plaintiff in the same area of the plaintiff’s established trade symbol; and
Defendant’s actions will likely cause consumer confusion as to the sponsorship of the good or service.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)

Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(3)(p), Fla. Stat. (four years); see [Ambrit, Inc. v. Kraft, Inc., 812 F.2d 1531, 1546 (11th Cir. 1986)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14024774320850500710). (3) Consent: like acquiescence, consent is defense where the licensor has expressly or impliedly consented to the infringement. See [Isaly Co. v. Kraft, Inc., 619 F. Supp. 983, 995 (M.D. Fla. 1985)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14403071572200541875); Restatement (Third) Unfair Competition § 29 (1995). (4) Abandonment: a defendant may raise the defense of abandonment when the plaintiff had previously abandoned the mark prior to making infringement claims against the defendant. See [Ambrit, Inc. v. Kraft, Inc., 812 F.2d 1531, 1546 (11th Cir. 1986)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14024774320850500710); see also 15 U.S.C. § 1127; Restatement (Third) Unfair Competition § 30 (1995).

Unreasonable Delay (Laches): inexcusable delay in bringing an action for infringement that results in prejudice to the defendant may serve to bar, in whole or in part, the plaintiff’s infringement claim. See [Ambrit, Inc. v. Kraft, Inc., 812 F.2d 1531, 1546 (11th Cir. 1986)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14024774320850500710); Restatement (Third) Unfair Competition § 31 (1995).

Plaintiff’s Misconduct (Unclean Hands): plaintiffs who seek a remedy in equity with “unclean hands,” which does not require the commission of a crime but only acts “condemned by honest and reasonable” persons, will be denied relief. See [Roberts v. Roberts, 84 So. 2d 717, 720 (Fla. 1956)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18417656984290964322); see also [Shatel Corp. v. Mao Ta Lumber and Yacht Corp., 697 F.2d 1352, 1355 (11th Cir. 1983)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12415193719808508275) (discussing unclean hands defense in trademark cases); Restatement (Third) Unfair Competition § 32 (1995).

Lanham Act (see 15 U.S.C. § 1115) defenses for incontestable trademarks: (a) mark was fraudulently obtained; (b) abandonment; (c) permission; (d) use is self-descriptive and in good faith; (e) adoption without knowledge of prior registration and continued use without objection; (f) prior registration under 15 U.S.C. § 1062, (g) mark is being used to violate antitrust laws; and (h) equitable defenses. See [In re Tampa Checkmate Food Services, Inc., 221 B.R. 541, 547 (M.D. Fla. 1998)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4214799699314369721) (statutorily enumerated defenses are not exclusive, and defendant may raise other defenses).

Plaintiff’s failure to initiate litigation against every potential and actual infringer does not, without more, diminish the strength of the plaintiff’s mark. See [Breakers of Palm Beach, Inc. v. Int’l Beach Hotel Dev., Inc., 824 F. Supp. 1576, 1584 (S.D. Fla. 1993)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2587169610121848110).

Protection is not available to generic marks that provide only information about the nature or class of service. See [Breakers of Palm Beach, Inc. v. Int’l Beach Hotel Dev., Inc., 824 F. Supp. 1576, 1584 (S.D. Fla. 1993)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2587169610121848110).

Acquiescence is an equitable defense available when the licensor has expressly or impliedly consented the infringement. See [Isaly Co. v. Kraft, Inc., 619 F. Supp. 983, 995 (M.D. Fla. 1985)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14403071572200541875).

Estoppel. See [Four Seasons Hotel and Resorts B.V. v. Consorcio Barr, S.A., 267 F.Supp.2d 1268, 1329-30 (S.D.Fla. 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16148818739047331539), aff’d in part, rev’d in part, 138 F. App’x. 297 (11th Cir. 2005) (Table, No. 03-16189).

See [Ambrit, Inc. v. Kraft, Inc., 812 F.2d 1531, 1546 (11th Cir. 1986)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14024774320850500710); Restatement (Third) Unfair Competition § 31 (1995). (6) Plaintiff’s Misconduct (Unclean Hands): plaintiffs who seek a remedy in equity with “unclean hands,” which does not require the commission of a crime but only acts “condemned by honest and reasonable” persons, will be denied relief. See [Roberts v. Roberts, 84 So. 2d 717, 720 (Fla. 1956)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18417656984290964322); see also [Shatel Corp. v. Mao Ta Lumber and Yacht Corp., 697 F.2d 1352, 1355 (11th Cir. 1983)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12415193719808508275) (discussing unclean hands defense in trademark cases); Restatement (Third) Unfair Competition § 32 (1995). (7) Lanham Act (see 15 U.S.C. § 1115) defenses for incontestable trademarks: (a) mark was fraudulently obtained; (b) abandonment; (c) permission; (d) use is self-descriptive and in good faith; (e) adoption without knowledge of prior registration and continued use without objection; (f) prior registration under 15 U.S.C. § 1062, (g) mark is being used to violate antitrust laws; and (h) equitable defenses. See [In re Tampa Checkmate Food Services, Inc., 221 B.R. 541, 547 (M.D. Fla. 1998)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4214799699314369721) (statutorily enumerated defenses are not exclusive, and defendant may raise other defenses). (8) Plaintiff’s failure to initiate litigation against every potential and actual infringer does not, without more, diminish the strength of the plaintiff’s mark. See [Breakers of Palm Beach, Inc. v. Int’l Beach Hotel Dev., Inc., 824 F. Supp. 1576, 1584 (S.D. Fla. 1993)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2587169610121848110). (9) Protection is not available to generic marks that provide only information about the nature or class of service. See [Breakers of Palm Beach, Inc. v. Int’l Beach Hotel Dev., Inc., 824 F. Supp. 1576, 1584 (S.D. Fla. 1993)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2587169610121848110). (10) Acquiescence is an equitable defense available when the licensor has expressly or impliedly consented the infringement. See [Isaly Co. v. Kraft, Inc., 619 F. Supp. 983, 995 (M.D. Fla. 1985)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14403071572200541875). (11) Estoppel. See [Four Seasons Hotel and Resorts B.V. v. Consorcio Barr, S.A., 267 F.Supp.2d 1268, 1329-30 (S.D.Fla. 2003)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16148818739047331539), aff’d in part, rev’d in part, 138 F. App’x. 297 (11th Cir. 2005) (Table, No. 03-16189).

title: Unjust Enrichment
description: Plaintiff has conferred a benefit on the defendant, who has knowledge thereof; Defendant voluntarily accepts and retains the benefit conferred; and The circumstances render the defendant’s retention of the benefit inequitable unless the defendant pays to the plaintiff the value of the benefit.
elements: Plaintiff has conferred a benefit on the defendant, who has knowledge thereof;
Defendant voluntarily accepts and retains the benefit conferred; and
The circumstances render the defendant’s retention of the benefit inequitable unless the defendant pays to the plaintiff the value of the benefit.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)

title: Usurious Transaction
description: “As a matter of law, a usury violation does not arise under an agreement. Rather it arises under state statutory law.” [BREA 3-2 LLC v. Hagshama Fla. 8 Sarasota, LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13704996647325063703), 327 So. 3d 926, 936 (Fla. 3d DCA 2021) (citing; [Party Yards, Inc. v. Templeton](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=14780717969288573942), 751 So. 2d 121, 123 (Fla. 5Th DCA 2000)). “Usury is a creature of statute. Thus, usury violations are statutorily governed and give rise only to those penalties and relief statutorily contained or provided. Other damages, compensatory or punitive, are not recognized or permitted.” [Cerrito v. Kovitch](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6913695284627041669), 423 So. 2d 1008, 1009 (Fla. 4th DCA 1982) (citing; [Moretto v. Sussman](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6065148626549758986), 274 So.2d 259, 260 (Fla. 4th DCA 1973)).
elements: There must be a loan express or implied;
An understanding between the parties that the money lent shall be returned;
That for such a loan a greater rate of interest than is allowed by law shall be paid or agreed to be paid, as the case may be; and
There must exist a Corrupt intent to take more than the legal rate for the use of the money loaned.
defenses: [R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: Stat. §95.11(3)(f) (four years).

The borrower has the burden of proving the elements of the alleged usurious transaction. Bardfield v. Chisholm Properties Cir. Events, LLC, 2010 WL 1688451, *6 (N.D. Fla. Mar. 25, 2010); Swanson v. Gulf W. Int’l Corp., 429 So. 2d 817, 819 (Fla. 2d DCA 1983).

Generally, ignorance of the law is not a defense for usury, even when the lender relies on the advice of counsel. [Saralegui v. Sacher, Zelman, Van Sant Paul, Beily, Hartman & Waldman, P.A.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3480109667751245471), 19 So. 3d 1048, 1053 (Fla. 3d DCA 2009); [Ross v. Whitman](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8829954364864109617), 181 So. 2d 701, 703 (Fla. 3d DCA 1966).

In Florida, civil usury laws are not applied to loans that exceed $500.000. If the interest rate exceeds 25% it is considered criminal usury. [Singhal v. Unison Agreement Corp.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8482482992289684136), 2023 WL 2734230, *4 (S.D. Fla. Mar. 31, 2023); [Top Beam Inc. v. ShieldX2 LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17913962408938748742), 2022 WL 2758386, *6 (S.D. Fla. June 28, 2022); Section 687.071, Fla. Stat.

“A borrower who asserts usury as a defense must prove all the elements of usury by clear and satisfactory evidence.” Bardfield v. Chisholm Properties Cir. Events, LLC, 2010 WL 1688451, *6 (N.D. Fla. Mar. 25, 2010) (citing; [Dixon v. Sharp](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=12305132374586902228), 276 So.2d 817, 819 (Fla. 1973)).
