title: Worthless Check
description: To recover the amount owing, treble damages, court costs, and attorney fees, the payee must also deliver a written demand to the drawer by certified or registered mail, evidenced by return receipt, at least 30 days before filing suit. §68.065(4).
defenses: [Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)
Statute of Limitations: §95.11(2)(b), Fla. Stat. (five years); [Sarras v. Mills-Sarras](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2672954576440307615), 161 So. 3d 509, 510 (Fla. 5th DCA 2014).
The written demand required by § 68.065(4) shall read substantially as follows:

“You are hereby notified that a check, draft, order of payment, debit card order, or electronic funds transfer numbered ___ in the face amount of $___ issued by you on (date), drawn upon (name of bank), and payable to ___, has been dishonored. Pursuant to Florida law, you have 30 days from receipt of this notice to tender payment in cash of the full amount of the dishonored payment instrument, plus a service charge of $25 if the face value does not exceed $50, $30 if the face value exceeds $50 but does not exceed $300, $40 if the face value exceeds $300, or 5 percent of the face amount of the dishonored instrument, whichever is greater, the total amount due being $___ and ___ cents. Unless this amount is paid in full within the 30-day period, the holder of the dishonored payment instrument may file a civil action against you for three times the amount of the dishonored instrument, but in no case less than $50, in addition to the payment of the dishonored instrument plus any court costs, reasonable attorney fees, and any bank fees incurred by the payee in taking the action.”

Section 68.065(3)(a) provides for the payment of the face amount of a worthless check, plus treble damages. [BEO Mgmt. Corp. v. Horta](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2683999888975181582), 314 So. 3d 434, 437 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020).

If the court or jury determines that defendant’s failure to satisfy the dishonored check was due to economic hardship, the court or jury has discretion to waive all or part of the statutory damages. §65.065(6); [Huston v. Plantation Open MRI, LLC](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=15619636263623834958), 66 So. 3d 1042, 1045 (Fla. 4th DCA 2011).

A defense available to a defendant charged criminally for issuing a worthless check is that the recipient of the check knew or had good reason to believe that, at the time the check was given, the funds at the bank were insufficient to cover the check. [Morin v. State](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16433992399687096434), 790 So. 2d 588, 589 (Fla. 5th DCA 2001).
Criminal sanctions provided in Section 832.07, Fla. Stat. may be applicable to violators of Section 68.065(3)(a).

After commencement of the action but before the hearing, the maker or drawer may tender to the payee, as satisfaction of the claim, an amount of money equal to the sum of the payment instrument, the service charge, court costs, and incurred bank fees. Other provisions notwithstanding, the maker or drawer is liable to the payee for all attorney fees and collection costs incurred by payee as a result of the payee’s claim. §65.065(6).

In actions where defendant stops payment on the instrument, Plaintiff must also show that payment has been stopped with an intent to defraud. §68.065(3)(a); [Wolf v. Habashy](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8770867594801699882), 361 So. 3d 379, 382 (Fla. 4th DCA 2023).

When an individual acting as the representative of another signs an instrument on behalf of the person or entity represented but fails to indicate that he or she is signing in a representative capacity, the represented person or entity is legally bound. Fla. Stat. §673.4021(1); [Big Bang Miami Ent., LLC v. Moumina](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8912250718615644545), 137 So. 3d 1117, 1119 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014).

title: Wrongful Birth
description: [Kush v. Lloyd](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18319149624536454308), 616 So. 2d 415, 417 n.2 (Fla. 1992); see also [Fassoulas v. Ramey](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17447735496381784807), 450 So. 2d 822 (Fla. 1984).
defenses: [Fla.R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)

Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(5)(b), Fla. Stat. (two years from the accrual of the cause of action. [Kush v. Lloyd](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=18319149624536454308), 616 So. 2d 415, 418 (Fla. 1992).

Statute of Repose: § 95.11(5)(c), Fla. Stat. (four years from the date the negligent advice is given). [Carr v. Broward Cty.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=11534223757898793950), 505 So. 2d 568, 569 (Fla. 4th DCA 1987).

“The cost of raising a previously unwanted but healthy and normal child is not a recoverable element of damages in a wrongful birth case.” [Health Tr. v. Brown](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2985897497862216852), 388 So. 2d 1084, 1084 (Fla. 3d DCA 1980).

“The impact rule should not be applied to actions for wrongful birth where emotional damages are the ‘parasitic’ consequence of conduct that itself is a freestanding tort.” [J. v. Humana of Fla.](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=606059254459782884), 652 So. 2d 360, 361 (Fla. 1995); see also [Gracey v. Eaker](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=3055939143119441105), 837 So. 2d 348, 356 (Fla. 2002).

“Ordinary rearing expenses for both a normal and defective child are not recoverable, and only the special expenses associated with raising a defective child to the age of majority are recoverable.” [Fassoulas v. Ramey](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=17447735496381784807), 450 So. 2d 822, 822 (Fla. 1984).

“Causation can be shown if the plaintiff can prove that she would have obtained an abortion if the doctor had not been negligent.” [OB/GYN Specialists of the Palm Beaches, P.A. v. Mejia](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6156057914455674068), 134 So. 3d 1084, 1087 (Fla. 4th DCA 2014).

Wrongful birth is a subset of medical malpractice and can only be brought against a health care provider as defined by the Medical Malpractice Act. See § 766.102, Fla. Stat.; see also [Shaffer v. Icely](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16053072712171768877), 16 So. 3d 282, 283 (Fla. 2d DCA 2009).

title: Wrongful Death
description: See Florida Wrongful Death Act: § 768.16 – § 786.26 Fla. Stat.
elements: Defendant owed a legal duty to the decedent;
Defendant breached that duty;
Defendant’s breach was the proximate cause of death; and
Damages.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See Chapter 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)

Statute of Limitations: § 95.11(4)(d), Fla. Stat. (two years). but see [Thomas v. City of Jacksonville, No. 3:13-cv-737-J-32MCR, 2017 WL 3316478, at *8 (M.D. Fla. Aug. 3 2017)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9270981747668843539). (stating “Claims for wrongful death brought against a natural person for an intentional tort resulting in death from acts described in s. 782.04 (murder) or s. 782.07 (manslaughter) may be commenced at any time.”).
Florida Wrongful Death Act: § 786.16 – § 786.26, Fla. Stat.

Contributory Negligence: The decedent’s contributory negligence may set off the award of economic damages. [Horton v. Channing, 698 So.2d 865, 866 (Fla. 1st DCA 1997)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1135859/horton-v-channing/); [Cody v. Kernaghan, 682 So.2d 1147, 1148 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2111587380462914746).

Committing Felony: Where the decedent dies while committing a felony, no recovery is permitted. See § 776.085(1), Fla. Stat. (6) Personal Representative: Only the personal representative of the decent may bring a wrongful death action, for the benefit of the decedent’s survivors and estate. See Linder v. DDR Realty Corp., 2015 WL 12791480, at *1 (S.D. Fla. May 12, 2015); [Williams v. Infinity Ins. Co., 745 So.2d 573, 576 (Fla. 5th DCA 1999)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=8100134682165648723); § 768.20, Fla. Stat.
Fetus: An unborn fetus is not a “person” under the Florida Wrongful Death Act. See[Duncan v. Flynn, 358 So.2d 178, 178 (Fla. 1978)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4618993554164053828).

The duty element of negligence is a threshold legal question; if no legal duty exists, then no action for negligence may lie. See [Jenkins v. W.L. Roberts, Inc., 851 So.2d 781, 783 (Fla. 1st DCA 2003).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=16516441420578117798)

Employers in compliance with the Worker’s Compensation Law are immune from claims for wrongful death, unless an intentional tort exception applies. § 440.11, Fla. Stat.; [Ramsey v. Dewitt Excavating, Inc., 248 So.3d 1270, 1272 (Fla. 5th DCA 2018).](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=6265654446944993737)

title: Wrongful Interference with Testamentary Expectancy
description: Generally, a claim for Wrongful Interference with Testamentary Expectancy does not accrue until after the testator’s death. See, e.g., [Whalen v. Prosser, 719 So.2d 2, 5 (Fla. 2d DCA 1998)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9606652851620555691); but see [Carlton v. Carlton, 575 So.2d 239, 240-243 (Fla. 2d DCA 1991)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=10582669663220952215)(only Florida court to allow pre-death claim).
elements: Plaintiff had an expectancy to be a beneficiary of and receive property from a testator’s estate;
Defendant intentional interfered with the expectancy through tortious conduct, including duress, fraud or undue influence;
Defendant’s actions caused Plaintiff to suffer damage; and
Plaintiff suffered damage.
defenses: [(1) Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.110(d) (pleading affirmative defenses), and other standard defenses. See § 1.](https://floridalitigationguide.com/fla-r-civ-p-1-110d-and-other-standard-defenses/)

Statute of Limitations: § 95.11, (3)(o), Fla. Stat. (four years). (3) If adequate relief is available in a probate proceeding, then that remedy must be exhausted before a tortious interference claim may be pursued. [Dewitt v. Duce, 408 So.2d 216, 218 (Fla.1981)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=9727752778416747289); Chauncy v. Gorden, No. 6:24-CV-573-RBD-EJK, 2024 WL 4793329, at *3 (M.D. Fla. Oct. 18, 2024).
